Welcome to the City of Southport!
The City of Southport was established in 1832 and was one of the first Marion Country communities to be incorporated in 1853. In 1969, Southport chose to be an “excluded” city within uni-gov, the consolidation of Indianapolis and Marion County governments, thereby retaining its unique presence on the edge of the big city. As of the census of 2020, there were 2,123 people, 763 households, and 733 families living in the city. If you are new to the city and would like to receive a Welcome Packet, please contact the mayor's office at 317.786.5489 to request one.

Tree Limb Disposal
Tree Limbs can be disposed of two different ways. One way is you can burn them if you adhere to the burn ordinance. items.title: Health Board Meeting Minutes 12-10-25
items.text: JOHNSON CO. HEALTH DEPARTMENT Environmental Health & FAX: (317) 736-5264 Vital Records Phone: (317) 346-4367 95 Drake Rd Email: csnider@JohnsonCounty.in.gov Franklin IN 4613 ahilton@ JohnsonCounty.in.gov jlashlee@JohnsonCounty.in.gov December 10, 2025 The Johnson County Board of Health meeting was held on December 10th, 2025, in the Health Department conference room. Those in attendance from the Board were Doctor James Pease (Chairperson), Susie Baker, Ruth Freese, Chele Heid and Dr. Mike Pauszek. Paul Hass, board attorney, also attended. Those in attendance from the Health Department were Dr. Qualls, Betsy Swearingen, Lisa Brown, and Cheryl Snider. The meeting began at 7:30 am. There was a motion to approve the minutes for the August meeting by Chele Heid and Dr. Pauszek gave a second to the motion. Another motion was made to approve the October minutes by Dr. Pauszek and Susan Baker gave second to the motion. Health Officer’s Report: Dr. Qualls stated we would be starting our performance reviews after the first of the year. He has looked online for a review specifically for health officers. He found something he could adapt to the job description. A couple of the items discussed were strategy, strategy formulation and strategy implementation. He then mentioned that the county government is pressing to give a large portion of our HFI funds to the Johnson Memorial Behavioral Health facility. He thinks once the facility is up and running, it will be greatly used. There is a great need for this type of facility. After pushing back many opening dates, it is hoped the center will be opened in January 2026. Nursing Report: We began STI testing in October. There were five Chlamydia and two were treated. Our walk-in clinics are on Mondays. Data entry for syphilis was rejected by the program. Apparently, the system is quite specific. If the data is not put exactly right, then it rejects the information. We have ten children going through the lead treatment program. There are three active TB cases, 43 patients being treated for latent TB. We administered five skin TB skin tests and 18 QuantiFERON (QFT). Nursing had 125 patients and 272 vaccines given, nine HIV tests and 1 Hep B. Lisa, Jaycie and Betsy met with the Johnson County Library to discuss a one stop service on 4 Saturdays in 2026. This would include TB testing, “Stop the Bleed” and CPR trainings. There have been many changes in the Nursing Division. Medical Assistant Sarah has left and is working from home. Our new Medical Assistant Cindy is running the clinics, administering vaccines and QFT. She is doing a great job. Environmental: Food renewals are coming in. We are trying to get into every food establishment this year. Our warehouses like Amazon are the hardest to get in to inspect. These places have vending machines that need to be inspected. We are not renewing Johnson’s BBQ’s license. Betsy went to close the place, however, the gentleman working asked to be given to the end of the year to get things fixed. Betsy obliged and gave them to the end of the year on the condition that the fix list had to be 100% completed. If not then we would terminate their license. Johnson County has a couple of new high-end restaurants. Mo’s in Greenwood and Gastro Pub in Franklin. Emergency Preparedness: We are in Q2 of our grant for emergency preparedness and have completed the requirements of meetings and exercises. Connie and Betsy are in the process of making sure all the supplies given out have receipts and had been sent to claims for 2025. Everything the fire departments asked for this year has been supplied. Those things include stretchers, medicine vaults for the ambulances, and even an automatic chest compressor. We’ve bought some cadaver bodies so the coroner’s office can do training with all county EMS personnel. Vital Records Deaths 116  Cancer Deaths 24  Suicides 1  Tobacco related 11 Births 29 Breast Cancer Awareness: We will not be renewing our Breast Cancer Awareness Grant for 2026. JoEllen is retiring and we do not have the staff to take over. We have several places we can refer a patient to. Community Health: Nothing reported. FHI: Connie and Betsy met with the state to go over the end of year financials. The Health Department has received an extra $11 thousand because another county opted out of the HFI program. We received a portion of that money. The funding is based on not every county spent their money in 2024. We accepted the money in 2025 and spent approximately 60% of the money. We will be giving Johnson Memorial about $150 thousand in rollover which will leave us to spend an additional $700 thousand in 2026. We are trying to be good stewards of the money. We have requested a meeting with the commissioners and the legal department to discuss how we would like to spend that money. Personnel: We tried to reclassify Connie’s job description based on the new ordinance passed by our County Council. The Auditor believes the job should be classified as exempt as Connie has a lot of overtime. The job description was rewritten and everything she does in her job was listed. It was sent to the Council, but no one replied. Her job description was compared to other office managers of her level and went through piece by piece. Every other department was paid higher. The Council refused to reclassify and there is nowhere to appeal. Our new School liaison will be starting December 2nd. Her name is Emma Dickens. New Business: Dr. Pauszek has been reappointed to the Johnson County Board of Health. Dr. Stropes is also up for re-appointment but has yet to fill out the form. One of the goals of the Health Department is to set up an indigent clinic for Franklin. The focus would be disease management for the underserved. This would include diabetes support, hypertension, COPD etc. Getting people their meds is hard and very costly. We can tap into some funds for that type of service. There was nothing else to discuss and the meeting was adjourned.

items.title: Health Board Meeting Minutes 2-25-26
items.text: JOHNSON CO. HEALTH DEPARTMENT Environmental Health & Fax: (317) 736- 5264 Vital Records Phone: (317) 346-4367 95 Drake Rd Email: csnider@JohnsonCounty.in.gov Franklin IN 4613 ahilton@ JohnsonCounty.in.gov jlashlee@JohnsonCounty.in.gov February 25, 2026 The Johnson County Board of Health meeting was held on February 25, 2026. Those in attendance from the Board were Dr. James Pease (Chairperson), Ruth Freese, Dr. Steven Stropes, Chele Heid, and Dr. Mike Pauszeck. Those in attendance from the Health Department were Ellizabeth Swearingen (Director), Bob Smith (EHS), Cheryl Snider (VRP-S), Jaycie Miller (Health Educator), and Lisa Brown (Nursing Director). The meeting started at 7:30 am. A motion to approve the December minutes was made by Dr. Stropes and a second was made by Dr. Pauszeck. Health Officer: Dr. Qualls could not be at the meeting, Betsy presented the report. She and Dr. Qualls have started performance appraisals for staff. There have been 4 completed and there is a March 2nd deadline for those interviews. The annual report is complete and ready for viewing. Every restaurant in Johnson County has had at least 1 inspection in 2025. There were a couple of breweries we realized we did not need to license. Planetary Brewing, as an example, does not serve food, therefore they do not need to be licensed by us. Breweries are different from establishments who sell beer. Nursing Report: This year, from January to date of report, there were 127 total patients with 257 vaccines. There are 22 children undergoing lead case management with a level of 5 mg/dl or above; eight are confirmed and are receiving treatment. The remaining 14 cases are still undergoing investigation whether it be retesting or blood drawing for confirmation. We have performed 3 lead checks. STIs include 5 HIV and 4 chlamydia and Gonorrhea. Someone is coming next week to receive testing for syphilis and HEP C as well. There are 2 active cases that were closed out at the end of the year. Currently there are no active cases. There are 57 patients who are undergoing treatment for latent TB. There are 16 immigration work ups. Kiley gets a report and is working with those immigrants. There were 8 QuantiFERON drawn up and 25 skin tests for TB. There has been an increase this season of individuals requesting influenza and Covid vaccines. Environmental Report: Bob Smith reported there are several new food establishments that have opened recently or are getting ready to such as the Chick -fil-A and Aldi here in Franklin. Kudos to Andrew Miller EHS who does all our plan reviews, remodels and pre-openings. He does a great job. The first festival of 2026 is going to be “DEATH & TAXES DAY” in Bargersville. The Whiteland High School has a new natatorium that will be opening soon. You can take a tour of that facility. It holds 700,000 gallons of water. It has underwater lights and sensors for safety issues. It has 24 drowning sensors. The new housing addition across from the Legends Golf Course will have a pool as well as the new apartment complex north of Franklin. There are some issues with housing and lodging. Hotels and motels used for emergency shelters will be evaluated on an annual basis whether they meet safety and sanitation measures. These are facilities which take in people in case of a weather disaster such as tornadoes and inclement weather. The Relax Inn had a roof collapse that damaged the plumbing. Therefore, it did not have a fire suppressant system. The owners were given the option to repair the building or have a 24-hour watch (fire personnel). They opted not to do anything and closed the property. It was put under a condemnation notice by the Health Department. There are also other places the Health Department is going to address. Extend Stay Greenwood is one and the apartments located at The Desperation Depot. Betsy and Bob were scheduled to go with the Sheriff’s Department to the apartments at The Desperation Depo but it snowed and they were unable to go. The Econo Lodge and Relax Inn on Umbarger Rd are two different properties even though they are linked together. We’ve never condemned by someone else’s code however, the fire departments stated it could not be opened because of lack of fire suppressant system. This is a facility used by the indigent community when shelter is needed. The Health Department is going back to the Econo Lodge, but Betsy does not feel it fits the description for being leveled. The Relax Inn on the other hand does fit the description and feels it would be better for the surrounding community if it were leveled. The Health Department would like to propose having a yearly inspection of these hotels that are used for emergency shelters. House Bill 1001: The bill states there will be no codes for new housing in housing additions. This undermines the Health Department, Planning and Zoning, housing codes and septic codes. Johnson Memorial Hospital is closing their maternity center. The Health Department is going to take a bit of a hit on that. There is also some language if you are the resident of a county, you should not have to pay for a birth record from that county. Every legislative person voted for this bill. So, the Indiana Legislature is not looking out for the health departments nor the Planning & Zoning department. The Health Department had its fee schedule approved at the last Commissioner’s meeting. The fee schedule needed to be revised in some areas such as fees, spelling and in general overall looks. It passed with no problem. Emergency Management: Betsy signed the letter of intent for BP3. It went before the Board of Commissioners and was passed. We are in the third year of the five-year cycle for BP3. The new cycle starts July 1st. Lisa and Betsy continue to go to Division 5 Preparedness Meetings. They are getting ready for a MSA (Metropolitan Statistical Analysis) tabletop exercise. It’s the CRI (City Readiness Initiative) through the CDC. A portion of what we get through the grant requires us to sit at a tabletop exercise with other MSA partners that are funded by the CDC. This will be in April. We’ve just concluded “Halo” training. It is a requirement in Johnson County for paramedics to attend these meetings. We used real cadaver bodies to simulate amputation, air way intubation practices, and a pare-mortem C-section with a 20-week-old fetus with a mother in cardiac arrest among other procedures. The State Medical Advisor attended and stated it was one of the best “Halo” training sessions he’d seen in the State of Indiana. There will be a resource rodeo in June presented by the D5 Health Care Coalition. This is for any health department, hospital or EMS, with resources to find supplies or equipment they might need. Vital Records: Births: November - 29 December - 52 Deaths: November - 117 December - 130  Suicide November - 1 December - 0  Tabacco related November - 11 December - 15  Drug related November - 0 December - 2 In April there will be the IVRA conference we will be going to. We are continuing to supply out of county death certificates. This seems to be very helpful to our funeral directors. Community Health: Since the beginning of the year, we have distributed 217 doses of Narcan. We have posted CPR training hosted by the Greenwood Fire Department. The classes have been well attended. We have been working closely with the Mobile Integrated Health Team. White River Township, Greenwood, and soon Bargersville have teams that implement programs throughout the communities and county wide. A meeting has been set up to hopefully have more of a county wide structure. Each community is unique in the way they do things. Jaycie is hoping to get some communication and collaboration as programs get up and running. Through meetings with EMS, it’s been interesting to hear the challenges they have with individuals and getting them resources. As the weather gets nicer, Jaycie is getting ready for community events which happen all the time in Johnson County. She feels it’s important to go out in the community and show people what the Health Department does for the community and where people can get help. We will be terminating our contract with Julota which is the software we’ve been using. We will be using Health Call instead as it will be much more user friendly. Health First Indiana: Betsy will be going to the Commissioner’s meeting on March 9th to discuss how to roll over the HFI funds for 2025. There will be about one million in roll-over funds. There will be no roll-over for 2026. After giving JMH the remainder of the roll-over for 2026 and anticipating the 2027 funds that were given plus and additional $165,000 will bring the total to one million for the next two years. It gave us approximately $800,000 to spread over 2026 & 2027. We are still looking to fund UPSTREAM and ASSIST. DRUG FREE INDIANA will receive $25, 00 from us and then $50,000 from the Opioid Settlement Funds. Tobacco Cessation has been removed from the core services of the HFI. We will have to figure out a different way to pay for that program. We will set aside some money for EMS so they can keep doing their programs like HALO and buying equipment for our EMS that don’t have the state-of-the-art equipment that they need. We are also hoping to expand the whole blood program. We would like to get JMH involved so we can switch out blood that is expiring. Board of Health Oversight: The budget passed. Dr. Qualls and Betsy are in the process of employee evaluations. There was no new business. The meeting was adjourned.

items.title: Health Board Meeting Minutes 4-22-26
items.text: JOHNSON CO. HEALTH DEPARTMENT Environmental Health & FAX: (317) 736- 5264 Vital Records Phone: (317) 346-4367 95 Drake Rd Email: csnider@JohnsonCounty.in.gov Franklin IN 4613 ahilton@ JohnsonCounty.in.gov jlashlee@JohnsonCounty.in.gov Board Meeting April 22, 2026 The Johnson County Board of Health Meeting was held on April 22, 2026. Those in attendance from the Board were Dr. James Pease (Chairperson), Ruth Freese, Dr. Steven Stropes, Chele Heid and Amanada Stevenson-Holmes. Board Attorney Paul Hass was also in attendance. Those in attendance from the Health Department were Betsy Swearingen (Director), Lisa Brown RN and Cheryl Snider VRP-S. The meeting began at 7:30am. A motion to approve the February minutes was made by Ruth Freese and a second to approve the minutes was made by Chele Heid. The motion passed. Executive Session: There was not a session. Health Officer Report: Nothing reported. Nursing Report: March through April 21, nursing did 100 patients totaling 119 vaccinations. Currently there are 20 open lead cases going through management. Their levels are above the 5 marker. 7 of those cases are confirmed, 13 are in different stages. They have done 2 lead tests in house in the past 2 months. STI testing took a surge in the last couple of months. 19 HIV with one positive prompted a referral so they could get treatment. 2 Hep C, and 14 of the 19 included gonorrhea with 2 positives. 7 were tested for syphilis. There is one active TB. All the contacts have been contacted and tested. One of the contacts was positive. 34 cases are latent. 21 QFTs were given and 43 TB skin tests. Environmental Report: We are working hard to make sure we stay current on our food inspections. Every place was inspected in 2025. The first quarter ended in March, and we are making sure all our quarterly inspections are up to date. Paul is no longer with the Health Department. He acquired another job in the private sector. We are now looking for someone to fill his position. We are trying to be very selective in the candidate for the position. This person must be someone who wants to focus especially on food as we have an abundance of restaurant facilities. We did not split up his work between the environmentalists as whoever we hire will acquire his lists. The environmentalists are visiting his places and keeping his area going until we can hire someone. Betsy has taken his indoor air and asthma cases, as that was her specialty as an environmentalist. Jaycie is also leaving us. She has taken a fellowship in a hospital in South Carolina. We will also be needing someone to fill her position. There is a lady in Bargersville who has taken advantage of the Health Department. They are a bar that’s in a space the Town of Bargersville would not zone the way she needed. She wanted a food permit from us, but we could not give her one unless she worked out of an approved commissary kitchen. She could do no food prep and no dishwashing at the Bargersville location. They did have a three bay sink but it’s only for cleanup. We found out they had been running the bar but had not been back to the commissary since January. The Health Department informed her there were restraints attached to the permit, and she needed to follow the rules for the permit. She stated since those restrictions were not printed on the permit, we could not legally enforce them. She ended up revising her menu and doing some needed work. Septic inspections are at a high currently. We are having issues with failing septic systems. It seems after the installer leaves and the Health Department leaves, the crew does bad things and does not follow through with directions. Thus, we’ve had a couple systems fail. It seems we may have to call a couple of the installers in for conversations. Not because of what they are doing but because they are not managing their crews. Emergency Preparedness: We participated in the City Readiness Initiative (CRI) tabletop exercise for HEP A. It focused on the administrative and financial area of our response to an emergency. Cassi and Connie participated as Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Starting July 1, Lisa will take over as the chairperson of our District 5 LHD group. She has been Vice Chairperson for several years. We are in BP2 cycle right now, so when BP3 starts, as Lisa takes over and takes some initiative, this will really help Betsy out. Lisa stated she enjoys doing this and working with the other counties. The D5 HCC has a warehouse of preparedness supplies here in Franklin. Agencies from all over the district can come and see where to get supplies. This will be June 12th of this year. We are helping to plan an exercise for an “Active School Killer” scenario. This year’s scenario will be at Indian Creek Jr./Sr. High school. This will be held during the summer to not disrupt school and scare children. There will be two active incidences going at once. One in the gym and the other will be in a school board type meeting. Chad, the police Chief for Clark Pleasant Schools, organizes this every year. Each year it gets bigger. We will be turning over our mobile command for them to use. June 1st, the county will drop Pulse Point. If you are CPR certified, you can download an app that notifies you if you’re close to someone that is in cardiac arrest. If you are close and are so inclined, you can then go to them and perform CPR until help arrives. It has a 400% better survival rate. This is a partnership with UPSTREAM PREVENTION and 911. Not all counties have this app, however it is a national app. It can be used anywhere in the United States. Vital Records: Deaths- January 110 February 92 March 118  January Homicide 1 Drugs 4 Tobacco related 10  February Suicide 3 Tobacco related 5  March – no statistics currently Birth- January 34 February 45 March 33 The front office served 1547 people in March. We issued 1376 death certificates within our jurisdiction and 168 birth records. Total money brought in from other county death certificates is $43,000.00. In the next few months, we will be updating our genealogy list in birth and death records. In May there will be a spring IVRA conference. It is a condensed learning experience for best office practices and policies. It will be held in Fishers. We are struggling to get our burial transit permits in from our funeral directors. This is a document we save as it is attached to the deceased death record. Now that funeral directors can get death records from other counties, we don’t always get the BTPs. The local health department can no longer make amendments to the birth record. Any amendment, no matter how minor, must be made through the court system. This practice is unreasonable for many families as they have trouble affording it. Community Health: Jaycie was out due to death in the family. No report given. Health First Indiana: We went before the Commissioners to let them know how we would like to spend the rollover money. They approved it. Contracts are posted for Empower Johnson County, Drug Free Johnson County, Johnson Memorial Behavior Health, Upstream and ASSIST. This is 1 million to JMH, $50,000 to ASSIST, $25,000 to Drug Free, $50,000 to Empower and to Upstream $75,000. We are currently in the process of buying a new storm siren for Prince’s Lakes. They currently do not have a working siren and have not for some time. We are looking at approximately $30,000 for that. We just bought Amity two sirens. Board of Health Oversight: Amanda designed an employee review form to help evaluate our staff. We gave the form to everyone and asked about their goals for the next year. Dr. Qualls and Betsy sat down and came up with a scoring method for the evaluations. Everyone except one has turned in their review with goals. It’s Betsy’s goal to be proactive rather than reactive. We are focusing on prevention and planning and policies. Betsy had been meeting once a month with the environmental staff to talk about what is going on with them and their jobs. She will now also be meeting with the vital records staff once a month to relay any information needed to enhance the operation of the front office. We also meet monthly for a whole office staff meeting. All this will help with communication between the different groups. Per the Board’s request, Paul Hass will be speaking with Dr. Qualls about his availability at the upcoming meetings. New Business: St. Thomas is having their 30-year anniversary open house. This is by invitation only and Betsy will not be able to go. She offered the invitation to anyone on the Board that would like to go. Adjourned: The meeting adjourned at 8:19 am.

items.title: Health Board Meeting Minutes 6-24-26
items.text: JOHNSON CO. HEALTH DEPARTMENT Environmental Health & FAX: (317) 736-5264 Vital Records Phone: (317) 346-4367 95 Drake Rd Email: vitalrecords@johnsoncounty.in.gov Franklin, IN 46131 csnider@johnsoncounty.in.gov jlashlee@johnsoncounty.in.gov ahilton@johnsoncounty.in.gov June 24, 2026 The Johnson County Board of Health meeting was held on June 24, 2026. Those in attendance from the Board were Dr. James Pease (Chairperson), Ruth Freese, Dr. Steven Stropes, Chele Heid and Susie Baker. Those present from the Health Department were Paul Haas (Attorney), Betsy Swearingen (Director), Dr. Jefferson Qualls (Health Officer), Lisa Brown RN (Director of Nursing), Bob Smith (EHS), and Cheryl Snider (VRP-S). The meeting began at 7:30 am. A motion to approve the minutes of the April meeting was made by Dr. Steve Stropes and a second was made by Cheli Heid. The motion passed. Executive Session: None Health Officer: Dr. Qualls apologized for poor attendance at the meetings over the past year, due to the responsibilities of his other jobs. He promises to improve. A problem for the Health Department currently, as he sees it, is poor leadership in the county. Financially, they have come down hard on us and it makes it difficult to recruit new employees and retain them. In the same manner, they do not allow us to promote as needed. This leaves the Health Department as a steppingstone for people to train and then move on to higher paying jobs. As an example, the Health Department hired a School Liaison for $44,000.00. Per the County Council, her pay should have been only $42.000.00 for her classification. They were not going to ask her to pay the difference back, however, she would not get a cost of living raise until her classification catches up to her pay. Betsy explained to the Council that she asks her employees to do more each day. More restaurants, more schools, hundreds of food trucks, more everything and the county wants them to do more without more pay. County officials replied, “employees should feel lucky to have a job”. Dr. Qualls and Betsy disagree with this mentality. If Bob Smith should leave tomorrow, she was told she could get two people for the cost of Bob Smith. She doubts that. She stated it is a slap in the face for 44 years of service to our county. She can replace him, but at an entry level salary of $57,000.00. The Environmentalists are considered “PAT 2” classification. There is wide discrepancy in what “PAT 2” is being paid and it needs to be reigned in. The county is in the red and will be over the next 3 years. They are taking the HD excise tax, roughly $88,000.00, and putting it into the general fund and there is nothing that can be done about it. Our State Health Officer, Dr. Weaver, is coming to visit us. The original date was set in July, however that date has been rescheduled to September. She would like to see our new building and our Health Department and what we do. Nursing Report: May and June saw a total of 73 patients and 154 Vaccinations. July and August will see an increase in those numbers for back-to-school shots. There are 14 open lead cases with 8 confirmed and 6 pending. We performed 6 blood lead tests over the course of these two months. We performed 16 HIV and 7 Hepatitis C tests. We performed 14 chlamydia and gonorrhea tests, and 7 tests for syphilis. We currently have 1 active TB patient, though they are still hospitalized in Marion County at this time; all contacts have received testing, one household contact was positive, and they will begin treatment for LTBI. There are currently 33 individuals receiving treatment for LTBI. We performed 17 QFTs and administered 24 TSTs. We collected 186 sharps containers and distributed 152. There are currently two travelers being monitored for symptom development as they have traveled to countries where there is currently an Ebola outbreak. They are very low risk and only have a few days left of their 21-day monitoring period. We, along with the Indiana Immunization Coalition (IIC) are hosting an after-hours vaccination clinic on June 30th here at the health department from 4 – 7pm. We have two more clinics scheduled, one in mid-August and the other at the beginning of October. Emma may have additional clinics at the request of the school districts. Environmental: We have 67 pool facilities which will have been inspected by Memorial Day weekend. We have a summer intern that will be inspecting pools this summer. 36 inspections have been completed to date. We are in the throes of festival season, Cassi and Caleb oversee mobile units. Each unit is inspected before a permit is issued and again at the respective festival. More and more people are calling in trash complaints on their neighbors and businesses. Emergency Preparedness: There will be a “call down” as a fulfillment of requirements to the funding of Emergency preparedness. An “Active Killer Exercise” took place at the Indian Creek High School in early June. This included agencies of police, sheriff, fire departments and EMS. We also launched “Pulse Point” in conjunction with the Active Killer Training. This is a new application which links certified CPR people with those around them that might be having a health crisis. If this is downloaded on your phone, it will alert you if someone around you needs CPR. If needed and you respond, CPR can be administered until emergency help can get to the patient. Johnson County recently had a Resource Rodeo. This was a one-stop location where emergency agencies can find resources for equipment and supplies that are owned by the D5 Health Care Coalition (HCC). Vital Records: Births for April through June 38. Due to the closure of the maternity center at Johnson Memorial Hospital, there will be no further birth reports unless there is a home birth or a birth in the ER Dept. there were 2 Paternity Affidavits completed and 392 Birth Certificates purchased. At our IVRA CONFERENCE, THE State has asked us not to amend any minor spelling errors on birth records for anyone over the age of 2yrs old without a court order. We disagree with this policy as it will put a hardship on anyone of low- income status or the elderly. We feel if we (or the State) have made any error we should fix it at no charge. We tried to do one, however were chastised by the State and strongly asked not to do it again. Deaths for April through June (to date) 281. There were 8 suicides during that time and there were 27 Tobacco related deaths. January through June 10th a total of $69,760.00 has been brought in from “out of County” death certificates. I have broken them down by county should you want to see them. In county death certificates have brought in $56,262.00. Community Wellness: Nothing reported. Board Oversight: Nothing to report currently. New Business: Congratulations to Dr. James Pease for 50 years of service in the medical field. Meeting was adjourned at 8:28 am.

items.title: Health Board Meeting Minutes 8-26-26
items.text: JOHNSON CO. HEALTH DEPARTMENT Environmental Health & Vital Records FAX: (317) 736-5264 95 S. Drake Road Phone: (317) 346-4367 Franklin, IN 46131 Email: vitalrecords@johnsoncounty.in.gov csnider@johnsoncounty.in.gov jlashlee@johnsoncounty.in.gov ahilton@johnsoncounty.in.gov August 26, 2026 Johnson County Board of Health Meeting The Johnson County Board of Health met on August 26, 2026, in the Health Department Board Room at 7:30 am. Those in attendance were Dr. Pease (Chairperson), Dr. Pauszek, Susie Baker, Ruth Freese, Chele Heid and Amanda Stevenson Holmes. Those in attendance from the Health Department were Elizabeth Swearingen, Dr. Qualls, Lisa Brown, Bob Smith and Cheryl Snider. Approval of June’s minutes: A motion was made by Chele Heid and a second was made by Susie Baker. The motion passed. Executive Session: No business at this session. Health Officer: Dr. Qualls moved his office to the nursing area. He has gained a new perspective on what they do. Dr. Qualls has given some thought to working with the hospital on chronic disease management. A better perspective for public health would be chronic disease prevention. He would like to focus on diet for longevity. The Health Department is looking forward to Dr. Weaver’s visit in September. There are several things he would like to speak with her about. Nursing: Cyclosporiasis is starting to take a decline in Johnson County. There were 9 cases. Annie currently has 8 lead cases open which she is investigating. She has 4 which still needs to be confirmed through follow-up. She did 3 tests here in July and August. The others were referred. Sexually transmitted infections:  12 HIV  8 Hep C  25 Chlamydia and Gonorrhea  20 Syphilis There are several repeat patients coming for testing. We give testing free and the question to the board was, what do we do with these repeat patients. Betsy suggested we reach the limit of what we have and then limit the “frequent flyers” to 1 per quarter. It will need to be included in the next fee schedule. There was 1 active TB in July and August to date, and 33 Latent. There is 1 ongoing case for TB. The patient has many ongoing health issues, one of which they thought was brain cancer. Come to find out, the patient had TB in the brain and throughout his body. Now he is on 12 months of treatment and is recovering. Kylie has another case which is ocular.  There are currently 33 patients being treated for TB.  31 QuantiFeron tests were given.  24 TB skin tests were performed.  The nursing division took 257 full sharps containers for disposal. Emma is our new school liaison and is doing a great job in ramping up our after-hours and weekend clinics. In office clinics saw 126 patients. Last week, at the Parks and Recreation clinic saw 70 patients. There will be another clinic in October at the Parks and Recreation building. Environmental: Bob reported that Johnson County has 700 food facilities with 25 plan reviews pending. Some are new establishments, others are remodels. Starting in January, mobile food trucks will need to get a state issued license. With this license a food truck will be able to go to any county in the state. The local county will be responsible for inspecting these trucks. The license will cost approximately $450.00, in which the county will get half. What is concerning is that there are a few mobile units banned in Johnson County. What is to stop them from going to another county and getting the license there and coming here. We are in the middle of mosquito season. People are encouraged to evaluate their property and dispose of items that contain standing water such as old tires etc. Every licensed pool has been inspected. There are 60 licensed outdoor pools. There were 37 pool closures over the summer for various reasons. The Health Department has a new instrument that can locate septic tanks and distribution boxes. This will come in handy to help construction companies from driving over and damaging septic locations and years from now be able to find the septics for older homes. There have been issues with cockroaches roaming from one house to another. With infestation, a house can be so infested that the cockroaches will leave one house, cross the yard, and go to the neighbor’s home. Our office is working with a landlord to get help for one individual who has COPD. We had a case of hoarding in which Animal Control removed 47 cats. The ammonia smell hit you from outside of the residence. They were indoor cats; however, they were so feral they had their own colony within the home. The cats were spraying the walls and baseboards. The mental health needs of the owner are important, and our office works with mental health providers in these types of situations. We must work with adult services and child services sometimes to get help for these individuals. We have a new environmentalist in the office. Lauren is doing an excellent job. She is helping us get caught up with inspections. She is also taking on some of what Jaycie Miller did as the Health Educator. She is working with stocking Narcan boxes and the Recovery Cafe’. Lauren learned that Johnson County has a higher rate of lung cancer than surrounding counties. She would like to work on prevention and work with the School Liaison on youth prevention programs. A while back our office had the Sheriff’s Department call us on a residence who was having a large party. They were serving food and liquor with no permits. It was $20 to enter the property as advertised. They need to have permits for the pool, food, and drinks. The property is owned by a 25-year-old Haitian with armed guards at the gates. There is some fear there is some immigration fraud happening. Other agencies are investigating also. On September 4th, the JC Library is sponsoring the “Longest Table”. This is to encourage the community to sit down and have a meal together. This is 16 tables of 8 bringing in food they have prepared at home to share with each other. The problem is this is an organized event which has no permit. They know better, so now its Greek’s Pizza. Even with the new rules from the State, you cannot do a pitch-in like this with the food being made in family homes. Food MUST be prepared at a qualified facility. Emergency Preparedness: Our office purchased Starlink, which is a satellite-based communication service that can be used if a tower goes down or something happens and there is no internet. We purchased 4 units. We will keep one, the county EMA Mobile Command will have one, Greenwood Hazmat will have one and the last will go to the Sheriff’s Department to be used by SWAY and the Bomb Squad. Training for this will be incorporated into the LEPC Full Scale Exercise on October 6th. With the rain received in the last few weeks, Johnson County did fine. Edinburg had a bit of an issue as their sewer and overflow are together. Some restaurants closed as their drains backed up, which is what they are instructed to do. The Health Dept. helped the town of Rocky Ripple with guidance on flooding. They needed help in getting their FEMA assessment done. It was a matter of direction on paperwork and who to call. Lisa Brown was voted in as our District 5 chair of the local health department committee. Lisa will be going to the Indiana Preparedness Symposium next week in Carmel. One of the topics will be how to evacuate a long-term care facility if needed. Vital Records: From June through August there were 179 deaths to date. Four are pending in July, August is not complete yet.  Tobacco 10  Child Death 1  No suicides or homicides There were 5 births in Johnson Co., all homebirths. Jodi will be going to the fall IVRA conference in October where she will take another certification test. Greenwood Health Care had a resident fall which resulted in death. The coroner was not contacted as she should have been per protocol. After much to do between the doctor and Coroner, an investigation into the issue was initiated and put on record. When no one can or will sign a death certificate, it comes to the Health Officer and Dr. Qualls was called on to sign the record. Community Health: Nothing to report currently. Health First Indiana (HFI): We are looking to change our Key Performance Indicators. There are some areas that we have not been focusing on since Jaycie left. Board of Health Oversight: None New Business: We are the lead sponsor for the Friday Night Football Game of the Week on Corn Country. We will be able to produce our commercials (anything we want to talk about) and they can run simultaneously with our billboards. We had mandatory ADA training. Now every employee will need to sign a statement stating they have been ADA trained. Our building has been built with ADA compliance, and our staff would help anyone with a disability get what they need. There will be some benefit time changes with exempt employees. They do not want exempt employees to take benefit time hourly. These exempt employees include Betsy, Lisa, Dr. Quall and our two nurses. The meeting adjourned at 8:45am.

items.title: News | Franklin Township Civic League
items.text:
Willa Mae Wolfe Community Service Scholarship
For the past 28 years, the Franklin Township Civic League (FTCL) has awarded a $1,000 scholarship to a graduating Franklin Township resident in recognition of outstanding community service. Through this scholarship, the Civic League continues its tradition of giving back to Franklin Township by recognizing a high school senior who has devoted time and energy to making a great township even better. The scholarship is named in honor of Willa Mae Wolfe, who was a founding Board member of the Civic League and the first editor (volunteer) of the Franklin Township Informer.
The Franklin Township Civic League is proud to announce that the applications for the 2026 Willa Mae Wolfe Community Service Scholarship are now available. The scholarship will be available to any Franklin Township resident who is in his or her senior year of high school and can be used at any accredited institution for education beyond high school, including vocational schools. The review criteria is based primarily on the individual’s volunteer contributions to the community, such as school, church, neighborhood and extracurricular activities, with an emphasis on community work directly benefiting Franklin Township. Students must have a “C” average to be eligible.
Applications for the Willa Mae Wolfe Community Service Scholarship are available at the guidance offices of Roncalli High School, Franklin Central High School, Lutheran High School and on the Civic League’s Facebook page and website at ftcivicleague.org. All applications must be postmarked or delivered to the Civic League office by June 8, 2026. Applications may be mailed to “Scholarship”, c/o Franklin Township Civic League, 8822 Southeastern Avenue, Indianapolis, IN 46239. Applications may also be placed in the drop box by the front door of the Civic League building. For additional information, please contact the Franklin Township Civic League at 862-1774, email us at Franklintwpcivicleague@gmail.com or visit www.ftcivicleague.org
Apply now!

items.title: Home | Franklin Township Civic League
items.text:
Franklin Township Civic League Welcomes You
Who We Are
The mission of the Franklin Township Civic League shall be to: provide a citizen’s voice in the short and long-term issues that impact the quality of life in Franklin Township; provide information to the members of the community on issues that impact the Township; advocate for citizen participation in the governance of the township; engage citizens in preserving and enhancing the township’s history, present and future.
What We Do
Land Use & Zoning Committee
This committee is comprised of individuals living or working in Franklin Township who volunteer to examine land use issues with a perspective which will benefit the long term best interests of the community to preserve and enhance Franklin Township’s quality of life.
The charge of the committee shall be to take action on behalf of the Civic League in the appropriate disposition of land use and zoning issues and related matters which come before the League or community and to provide assistance and information to residents and businesses which enables understanding of and participation in land use and infrastructure matters.
The Land Use Committee meets on the third Wednesday of each month at 6:30PM in the Civic League Community Building in Wanamaker. The meetings are open and the community is welcomed and encouraged to
attend.
Building Committee
The Building Committee works to maintain the physical condition of Civic League building and to coordinate use of the community room by Franklin Township organizations. If you are interested in booking the room, you can make a reservation by clicking on our Calendly link here:
https://calendly.com/franklintwpcivicleague/franklin-twp-civic-league-community-room-rental
Newspaper Committee
The members of this committee, consisting of Board Members, community volunteers and the Editor of The Franklin Township Informer, are charged with contacting homes and businesses to make them aware of Civic League activities. They also work to offer League membership to all
Ways and Means Committee
This committee is composed of volunteers from the community and Civic League Board Members who work to coordinate fund-raising events which help support the activities of the League and allow the League to make significant financial contributions to the community and it’s organizations and events.
Membership Committee

2025-2026 Season Review
The Royal Boys wrapped up their 2025-2026 season with a 5-5 record, similar to their 2024-2025 performance. The team welcomed several newcomers to the team, and they all showed great improvements throughout the season. Sophomore Nathan Bastin was named to the Indy South All-Conference Team after his outstanding performances throughout the season. Seniors Andrew Woodruff , Emmett Burkhardt , Ethan Lentz and Sam Matney all earned Academic All-State honors, which recognized their achievements on the lanes and in the classroom. The Royals look forward to returning to the lanes next season to continue their progress.

items.title: Boys Basketball - Roncalli High School Athletics
items.text:
Boys Basketball
2025-26 Season Review
The Royals entered this season with championship aspirations, and they finally were able to achieve some goals that have been on their list for a few years. The team has been building towards this for a few years as a program, and it felt great! Led by their five seniors, Luke Baker, Brayden “BC” Collins, Luke Feldman, Conner Kesler & Joe Taylor , this 18-win, sectional & regional championship team was an entertaining one to watch.
Some season highlights included:
Started the season 6-0 (including a win over 2025 4A State Champs, Jeffersonville and 2026 4A Regional Champ, Decatur Central)
A road win at New Pal, after losing five straight to the Dragons over the last four years
Advancing to the sectional finals for the third year in a row
Winning three games and a sectional title by an average of 13 points
Beating higher-ranked Northview in the regional 54-43
18 wins – highest win total since 2017-2018 season
Joe Taylor set a school record for rebounds in a career with 535 rebounds
Junior Will Hegwood set a school record for assists in a career with 300 assists, and he still has one more season to play
Service Projects with Beggars for the Poor and Wishing Well
Conner Kesler and Joe Taylor selected for the Circle City All-Conference Team
Will Hegwood and Conner Kesler selected as Honorable Mentions on All-Marion County Team
Joe Taylor selected as an All-Marion County 2nd Team.
Joe Taylor selected to play in Marion County Senior All-Star Game
Senior leadership was at the forefront this season, and this group of boys will be missed by the program. Joe Taylor averaged 12 points and 7.5 rebounds per game while shooting 56% from the field, all while being really valuable defending the paint. Conner Kesler was the team’s leading scorer both his junior year and his senior year. He averaged 14 points per game and grew into a real leader for the Royals, and he was willing to do anything it took to win the game. Conner hit 93 three-pointers over his last two seasons and will certainly be missed. Luke Feldman led the team with 57 made threes this season, while shooting them at 43%. He was way more than just a shooter for the Royals, but his game winning three at New Pal will be remembered for a very long time! He will go down as one of our most efficient scorers in school history. Luke Baker grew into a super valuable part of our team. He was our starting four man, who was our second-leading rebounder, second in assists, and he usually guarded the opponents best player. “Bake’s” energy and spirit will be greatly missed! Brayden Collins provided everyday leadership with his approach and encouraging, helping voice. The ‘Best Teammate’ award-winner was always ready when his name was called, and he had a huge three pointer against Perry Meridian that nobody in the gym will ever forget. items.title: Baseball - Roncalli High School Athletics
items.text:
Baseball
2026 Season Review
The 2026 season was another strong year for Roncalli baseball, and winning a third straight Circle City Conference championship was a great way to cap it off. With the conference coming to an end, it means a little more to walk away as the final champions. A number of players were recognized for their performances this spring. Seniors Collin Ash and Luke Baker , along with juniors Gio Ardizzone, Ayden Hartman and Luke Roeder , were named All-Circle City Conference.
Ash, Baker and Ardizzone also earned First Team All-Marion County honors, while sophomore Dane Burton was named Honorable Mention All-Marion County. Collin Ash will also represent Roncalli in the Indiana All-Star Game after being selected to the South team as an All-District Outfielder.
The Royals finished the year with a 20-6 varsity record and a 14-8 JV record. The expectation in the program is to compete for championships every year, and the team is already looking forward to getting back to work for next season.
End-of-season Roncalli awards went to the following Royals:
MVPs: Collin Ash and Gio Ardizzone
Mental Attitude Award: Senior Max Kriner
Leadership Award: Collin Ash

Approx. 3855 Olive Branch Road, Greenwood VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow a group home use for senior living (not permitted in an SR, Single Family Residential District) V-13-26. Nineveh Township Volunteer Fire Dept. Approx. 8050 S. Nineveh Road, Nineveh. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow for the following: 1. Chapter 3, Section B, 5, b: To omit the required 6-inch continuous concrete curb around the parking lot perimeter separating paved from non-paved surfaces. 2. Chapter 3, Section C, 5, c: To omit the required perimeter landscaping and buffering standards surrounding the parking lot. OLD BUSINESS None. NEW BUSINESS Status update V-7-26. Sandhu Properties Inc. 5362 Warrior Trail. Whiteland REPORTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS None. ADJOURNMENT The next regular meeting of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals is scheduled for Tuesday, September 25th, 2026, at 7:00 PM. LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) 2 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-1-26 ADDRESS: 4912 Olive Branch Road, Greenwood 46143 (parcel #: 41-09-32-014-001.000-034) PETITIONER: Darren Poynter, Vickie Poynter by David Gilman REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance legally allows a 2,400-square-foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 3,150 square feet in building area. (The zoning ordinance allows aggregate accessory structure area to be no more than 100 % of the building area of the primary dwelling, or, in this case, 1,360 square feet). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 0.94-acre site is zoned SR (Single Family Residential) and improved with a residential home and two additional structures. The property is surrounded are similar-sized parcels used for residential on the north side of Olive Branch Road and larger lots used for residential on the south side of Olive Branch Road. Update for July Meeting The petition was continued at the April 28th 2025 meeting with the following motion: To continue V-1-26 to the July 27, 2026 meeting. The motion was based on staff recommendation since construction has not yet commenced and the violation remains on the property. As of July 21st 206, only some site preparation has occurred on the property. On 7/15/26, the property owner provided the following email from their subcontractor From: Cindy Fikes <cindy@mooreconstructionservices.net> To: Vickie Poynter <poynterv@sbcglobal.net> Sent: Tuesday, July 14, 2026 at 02:46:45 PM EDT Subject: Re: E-gress Info Hi Vickie, We are looking at 8/3 to get started on the foundation. I will let you know if we have any weather delays. Typically Daniel Cornett, the Stormwater specialist likes to come out before the digging starts. I will have Ian(Ken refers to him as Wes which is his middle name) reach out to Daniel a few days before we are getting started so he can meet him on site to discuss drainage, concrete clean out bags, etc. Once Brian our concrete guy gets started on the digging, we will coordinate the footer inspection which is when they come out to inspect the holes and make sure they are deep and wide enough before we pour concrete and start to install block. Thank you, Cindy Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 60-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and shows evidence to resolve the existing violation. Update for April Meeting The petition was continued at the January 27, 2026, meeting with the following motion: 3 “To continue V-1-26 for ninety-one (91) days to allow the Petitioners to present compliant building plans and to remove spoils from the property.” Since the January meeting, the property owner has applied for and was issued a building permit in April for a primary residence addition. Once constructed, this addition will increase the square footage of the primary structure sufficiently to allow for the larger accessory structure currently under dispute. If the addition is completed, the requested variance will no longer be necessary. However, as construction on the addition has not yet commenced, the violation remains on the property. Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 90-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and show evidence to resolves the existing violation. Regarding the second part of the motion, staff will provide an update at the meeting. VARIANCE REQUEST This variance request seeks approval to classify an existing 2,400-square-foot building as an accessory dwelling, despite it exceeding the maximum allowable square footage for accessory structures on a single tract of land. Under the current Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the total area of all accessory structures is limited to the size of the primary residence. On this specific property, the primary dwelling measures 1,360 square feet. Because there is already an existing 750-square-foot detached garage, the addition of this 2,400- square-foot structure significantly exceeds the permitted allotment. The history of this structure began in June of 2023 when the property owners applied for a building permit for a primary dwelling addition following consultations with county staff. Due to the scale of the proposed project, the owners submitted plans depicting an attached addition rather than a detached building. The design featured a fully enclosed breezeway intended to connect the 2,400-square-foot structure to the main house. However, the connection was never built. As the permit neared expiration, staff notified the owners that failure to construct the breezeway resulted in a zoning violation, as the building remained a non-compliant detached structure. While several options exist to bring the property into compliance, the owners have chosen to seek a variance to bypass the requirement for the connecting breezeway. It is worth noting that when this project was initially permitted, the previous zoning ordinance was even more restrictive, limiting accessory structures to 50% of the primary dwelling's size and requiring that they not exceed the height of the main house. Both the previous and current standards are designed to ensure that accessory buildings remain secondary to the primary residence and preserve the character of single-family developments. Large, oversized accessory structures often fail to blend with neighborhood aesthetics and can inadvertently encourage land uses that are not typically permitted within residential districts. FINDINGS OF FACT: VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The structure will not impact public health, safety, morals, or general welfare, as it will be verified that it is built to local and state building codes. 4 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. This oversizing is inconsistent with the established single-family character of the adjacent properties, there are no similar size structure in the area. A variance of similar requests could be sought by other property owners based on the same findings presented by the petitioner. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will not result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. The petitioner has failed to demonstrate that there are unique physical circumstances or conditions particular to this specific parcel of land—such as irregular lot shape, exceptional topography, or pre- existing infrastructure—that prevent them from adhering to the established development standards for an accessory structure. The petitioner presented building and site plans that would achieve the standard set forth and attainable. The Petitioner’s findings of fact list the distance and elevation as problematic; the property owner decided to locate the structure in that spot. 4. The variance is not primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. While economic benefit is present with this variance and could be a secondary consequence, it is not the primary motive for the variance. 5. The variance request is not the minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. The applicant has failed to present compelling reasoning that the entire amount of the requested variance is essential to overcome the physical hardship. No data was presented demonstrating that a smaller, compliant, or near-compliant structure would not serve the basic intended purpose. Specific justification for the size has not been adequately documented or presented as a necessity that overrides the zoning standard. The request appears to be driven by desire rather than an absolute, physically necessary requirement. 6. The variance request is due to hardship caused by the current owners of the property. The petitioner had reasonable and feasible design options available that would have satisfied the ordinance requirements or substantially minimized the deviation sought. The pursuit of a non-conforming design, despite clear alternatives, means the hardship is one of choice or preference, not one inherent to the land itself. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: David Gilman 211 S Ritter Avenue, Ste H Indianapolis IN 46219 Owner: POYNTER DONALD L & POYNTER DARREN E & POYNTER VICKIE L 5035 Cordia CT Indianapolis, IN 46237 5 Current Zoning: SR (single-family residential ) Existing Land Use: Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential -MNH 6 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-09-26 ADDRESS: 378 & 354 Western Blvd, Greenwood & Lot 4 of the Fairview West Commercial Subdivision, Parcel #: 41-03-33-021-027.000-038 and 41-03-33-022-006.000-038 PETITIONER: BLF Acres LLC, By Bill Niemier REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) to allow for the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within the Corridor Overlay District (COD), where such uses are prohibited. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION The subject property comprises two lots within the Fairview West Commercial Plat, located east of Interstate 69 (I-69) along Western Boulevard: Lot 3: 2.04 acres, currently improved with a vacant commercial building originally developed in 1997 as a fueling station and restaurant. Lot 4: 3.24 acres, currently undeveloped. These lots are not contiguous and are separated by Western Boulevard. Both lots are zoned GC (General Commercial) and fall within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Surrounding properties consist of commercially developed lots of similar size and character. VARIANCE REQUEST The applicant proposes to operate a business focused on the sales, repair, and rental of trailers and golf carts, as well as the installation of truck beds. Under the UDO, this activity falls under Automobile/Vehicle Sales, Rental, Service, and Repair. This category is explicitly listed as a prohibited land use within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Trailers would involve bumper-mounted flatbed, utility, car hauler, and enclosed trailers. It would not involve travel/recreational trailers or boat trailers. Historically, Western Boulevard connected directly to Fairview Road, a major commercial arterial adjacent to former State Road 37. During the conversion of SR 37 into I-69, the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) permanently closed three intersections within unincorporated Johnson County, including the SR 37 and Fairview Road interchange. This closure altered local circulation patterns, reduced direct passerby traffic, and contributed to business relocations in the immediate area. In anticipation of I-69, Johnson County partnered with a planning consultant to develop the I-69 Corridor Plan, which was adopted in December 2018 as a supplement to the Johnson County Comprehensive Plan. The plan aimed to establish high-quality architectural and land-use standards for the I-69 gateway into the county, explicitly identifying certain vehicular-oriented commercial uses as undesirable for new development. When the county adopted the updated Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) in 2024, these plan recommendations were codified into the Corridor Overlay District (COD) regulations. The COD establishes elevated design and development standards for sites, structures, landscaping, signage, and site improvements within highly visible county corridors to: 7 Promote High-Quality Design: Encourage creative, innovative, and visually cohesive site and building development. Protect Property Values & Welfare: Preserve long-term property values and promote public health, safety, and welfare through consistent, coordinated development standards. Ensure Efficient & Coordinated Development: Establish high standards that optimize land use, permit flexible site design, and protect the functional integrity and visual character of major transportation corridors. Because the COD regulations explicitly prohibit automobile sales, service, and repair, the proposed operation requires Use Variance approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals. The Future Land Use Map within the I-69 Corridor Plan designates this immediate area for Residential development. However, staff believes this designation was an analytical oversight during the 2018 planning process, as this specific node south of Fairview Road contains existing, built-out commercial development that is not discussed or recommended for residential transition elsewhere in the document. Staff feels a Mixed-Use designation would have been more appropriate for this node. The overall narrative of the I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly seeks to maintain economic vitality and support the adaptive reuse of existing commercial properties impacted by INDOT access closures along secondary frontage networks. While general commercial reuse of this built-out site aligns with the plan's economic vitality goals, auto sales and repair specifically are restricted by the COD regulations to uphold the corridor’s elevated visual standards—hence the necessity of the requested Use Variance. While this report focuses primarily on the land use request, any future development of the vacant Lot 4 will be subject to the standard Site Plan Review process. Lot 4 must adhere to all UDO development standards. Staff notes that the preliminary layout shown on the submitted site plan will likely change once formal site development and drainage requirements are fully engineered. No Development Standard Variances are requested at this time, as the petitioner wishes to secure land use approval prior to committing to full site engineering. To address potential visual impacts on the corridor without requiring immediate development variances, Staff has drafted specific conditions of approval aimed at managing outdoor staging and display areas. STAFF RECOMMENDATION Should the Board move to approve this request, Staff recommends the inclusion of the following commitments/conditions: 1. Lot 4 Use Restriction: Lot 4 shall be utilized exclusively for product display and staging. 2. Surfacing Requirement: Any development or staging area on Lot 4 shall be constructed with a hard, durable surface. 3. The product display and staging area shall be subject to the same standards as a parking lot, especially Chapter 3 Section 3,c and Section B,5,b,c and Chapter 3 Section C,5,c. Staff would strongly suggest considering interior landscaping as well if the paved area is to be over 1.5 acres. 8 4. Fencing Standards: If fencing is installed on Lot 4, chain-link fencing (with or without barbed wire) is strictly prohibited. Fencing must consist of wrought iron or high-quality privacy fencing materials. 5. No Outdoor Storage of Repair/Parts: No outdoor storage of items awaiting repair, salvage parts, or loose materials shall be permitted on either parcel (Lot 3 or Lot 4). FINDINGS OF FACT: USE VARIANCE State Requirement: The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The subject site includes an existing, vacant commercial building on Lot 3 originally developed in 1997. Granting a Use Variance to allow the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within this existing structure returns a vacant property to productive commercial use. Furthermore, restricting Lot 4 strictly to a heavily conditioned, high-quality staging and display area (or leaving it undeveloped) prevents unmitigated commercial expansion, thereby safeguarding the visual environment, public safety, and general welfare of the corridor. State Requirement: The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Reoccupying the vacant building on Lot 3 eliminates a long-standing vacancy that risks becoming a visual blight along Western Boulevard following INDOT's access closures. Surrounding properties are established commercial lots of similar character. By revitalizing the existing structure, the variance stabilizes local property values. To protect adjacent parcels from potential visual degradation associated with expanding commercial operations, approval is tied to strict conditions that prohibit open storage of parts or items needing repair and ensure that any use of the vacant Lot 4 is strictly limited to screened display rather than intensive site development or heavy industrial staging. State Requirement: The need for the variance arises from some condition peculiar to the property involved. The property features a unique duality: a fully built-out commercial structure (Lot 3) that was rendered vacant and functionally isolated due to INDOT's closure of the Fairview Road/SR 37 intersection, paired with an adjacent undeveloped parcel (Lot 4) separated by a public road. The existing building was constructed under prior standards for vehicular commercial activity, making its footprint well-suited for adaptive indoor reuse. However, the 2024 Corridor Overlay District (COD) standards strictly prohibit these land uses. This structural layout—a purpose-built commercial building stranded by transportation network changes—creates a unique hardship that can be remedied by allowing indoor adaptive reuse without endorsing the unrestricted build-out of the adjacent undeveloped land. State Requirement: The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which a variance is sought. Strict enforcement of the Corridor Overlay District (COD) prohibition against vehicle sales and service would prevent the economic reuse of a purpose-built, 2.04-acre commercial site (Lot 3) that already possesses the necessary building footprint and pavement. Forcing this established building to remain vacant—particularly after state-initiated access closures reduced passerby traffic—imposes an unnecessary economic hardship. Allowing the requested use inside the existing structure relieves this hardship while preserving the Board's discretion to apply strict development standards or limitations on the undeveloped Lot 4 to prevent unnecessary visual appearance. 9 State Requirement: The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly encourages economic vitality and the adaptive reuse of existing commercial inventory impacted by I-69 access modifications along secondary frontage roads. While the plan seeks to prevent the uncontrolled proliferation of roadside vehicle lots along the corridor, permitting the adaptive reuse of the existing structure on Lot 3 directly fulfills the plan's economic revitalization goals. By capping the intensity of the use and enforcing strict design and buffering standards on any proposed staging on Lot 4, the approval honors both the plan's economic goals and its intent to elevate the visual gateway standards of Johnson County.. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 2.56-acre site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and one accessory structure. The area surrounding this parcel consists of parcels of similar size, all used residentially. The properties directly to the west are located within the municipal limits of the town of Bargersville. VARIANCE REQUEST – DEVELOPMENT STANDARD The applicant is requesting a Variance of Development Standard to allow the construction of a 2,952-square-foot accessory structure on the subject property. The site currently contains two accessory structures: a 1,440-square-foot detached garage and a 96-square-foot shed. With the addition of the proposed 2,952-square-foot building, the total aggregate area of all three accessory structures would be 4,488 square feet. This exceeds the square footage of the primary dwelling, which is 2,912 square feet.
