items.text: Page 1 of 2 GREENWOOD COMMON COUNCIL RESOLUTION NO. 26-11 A RESOLUTION ESTABLISHING HOLIDAYS FOR EMPLOYEES OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD FOR THE YEAR 2027 WHEREAS, pursuant to Greenwood Municipal Code (1993), as amended, § 2-68(b), the Mayor and Common Council of the City of Greenwood, Indiana, are to establish holidays for the year 2027 by resolution on or before the last regular meeting of the Common Council in the year 2026; WHEREAS, Greenwood Municipal Code § 2-68 requires the Common Council to state by resolution each year which Actual Holidays the City will celebrate and the days upon which those Actual Holidays will be recognized. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA, THAT: Section 1. The City shall celebrate the following twelve (12) Actual Holidays in 2027: 1. New Year’s Day 7. Veteran’s Day 2. Presidents’ Day 8. Thanksgiving 3. Good Friday 9. The day after Thanksgiving 4. Memorial Day 10. Christmas Eve 5. Independence Day 11. Christmas Day 6. items.title: 9.19.26 Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council REVISED DRAFT MINUTES
items.text: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council MINUTES Date: September 21, 2026 Time: 7:00 pm Place: Council Chamber 300 S Madison Ave Greenwood, Indiana I. Call Meeting to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Prayer: David Denny - lay leader at Victory Baptist Church C. Roll Call: Council Members Present: Mike Campbell ("Mr. Campbell"), Linda Gibson ("Ms. Gibson"), Ezra Hill ("Mr. Hill"), David Hopper ("Mr. Hopper"), Erin Kasch ("Ms. Kasch"), David Lekse, ("Mr. Lekse"), Teri Manship, ("Ms. Manship"), Steve Moan ("Mr. Moan") Darin Hoggatt ("Mr. Hoggatt") City Officials: Mark Myers (“Mayor Myers”) Jeannine Myers ("Ms. Myers") Clerk, Greg Wright ("Mr. Wright") Controller, Sam Hodson (“Mr. Hodson”) Corporation Council, James Ison ("Chief Ison") Police Chief, Jayme Washel (“Chief Washel”) Fire Chief, Drew Foster (“Judge Foster”) City Judge, and Department Heads. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. This will be read before each meeting: Before we begin, I want to remind everyone that respectful participation is expected. We welcome public input at the appropriate times, but there will be no yelling or interruptions that prevent the meeting from moving forward. Anyone who disrupts the meeting will be asked to leave and may be escorted out. II. Approval of Minutes A. Minutes from the regular meeting September 9 ,2026 Motion to approve regular meeting minutes from September 9, 2026 by Kasch, seconded by Hill Votes: Ayes – Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper Kasch Abstain: Lekse, Manship, Moan, Hoggatt Motion Passes: 5-0 with 4 abstentions III. Reports A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Committee & Board Report IV. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit Deann Lautenbach, 2255 S. Franklin Rd, Greenwood, IN 46143 I live at the corner of Franklin and Clark Road in Greenwood. I'm an aggravated and affected neighbor due to living in the middle of the unfinished corridor between 65 and 74, which will be feeding an enormous amount of traffic to the destination travel center, being one of the largest gas stations in the entire state of Indiana. I am here tonight to establish a formal legally binding administrative record against docket PC 2026-035. To fully preserve my right to file a judicial review in the Johnson County courts. I request that this Council table this back to the Planning Commission or deny this petition because it creates a severe procedural violation, breaks local ordinances, and creates a textbook, arbitrary, capricious action. Indiana open door law. Under Indiana Code Section 5.14 1.55, public agencies are required to give public notice of their meetings, including posting an agenda if one is utilized at least 48 hours in advance, excluding weekends and legal holidays, dropping a major, unvetted, supplemental traffic study on a Friday afternoon for a Monday vote, actively circumvents the transparency mandated by the state sunshine law. Greenwood Planning Division staff report ruled: after an examination of information in the public record and findings from additional research, staff shall publish a technical review committee report that provides an analysis of the petition request. Such reports shall be published along with an agenda approximately five days prior to the meeting. By failing to give a five-day buffer, the city directly broke its own local guidelines. Indiana Code Section 3674607. This statute dictates that any zoning ordinance or planned unit development text amendment must follow a strict process between the Planning Commission and the Legislative Council. Under Indiana Land Use law, if a developer introduces significant technical updates or modifications after the Planning Commission has already voted, the Common Council is legally required to remand the proposal back to the Planning Commission. This ensures that the public hearing body can officially investigate, review, and certify the new data before a final vote takes place. Indiana Code Section 3674604. This statute mandates that a major zoning ordinance or text amendment cannot be legally enacted without a formal, legally advertised public hearing because the brand-new September 15th traffic memo reveals a severe level of service F gridlock. Failures right at our local school entrances, avenues, and because this data was hidden from the public portal until Friday afternoon, the community has never been granted a valid public hearing on the actual material facts of this case. I gave you guys all exhibits. Exhibit A: The build, this is from the traffic study, build 2037 capacity reports from Section F, all the traffic study. This document proves that the intersection of Emerson Avenue and Worthsville Road will suffer complete gridlock during peak morning school hours. The northbound approach drops to a level of service grade F, forcing parents, teachers, and school buses to face a catastrophic average delay of 275.26 seconds, which is over four and a half minutes. Of forced idling per vehicle. This extensive line of cars will stack directly backward during the morning peak hour, clogging the entrance avenues of Clark Pleasant Middle School and creating a dangerous hazard gridlock where student commuters are trapped in stationary traffic. Exhibit B: The existing 2026 plus site capacity reports from Section D of the study. This proves that the infrastructure will fail on day one. The very moment this site opens, page two reveals that the southbound approach directly exiting the Grassy Creek Elementary School access road completely breaks down into an immediate level of service F, forcing parents and school buses to idle for 74.9 seconds, over a minute each just to exit the school gates. Furthermore, page four exposed a catastrophic four-way systematic breakdown at county roads. 200 East and Worthsville Road, where the northbound and southbound approaches simultaneously fail at level service F, blocking up primary school access road with immediate delays up to three and a half minutes. Exhibit C, and I have more, but I can't. proving the developers actively breaking our local laws to circumvent safety protections, unifying development ordinances section 100107 with the illegal spot zoning. That's going on. I need to put that in the record so I can file a judicial review. Furthermore, your master plan used on table 17 completely bans travel plazas. That is illegal spot zoning. The developer is also proposing to remove an active timed travel traffic signal along the corridor and replace it with a roundabout element, eliminating the only mechanical guarantee that stops commercial traffic to let parents in school buses. Thank you. Kim Crawford, 166 Caplinger Place, Greenwood, In 46143 I am also the school board president for the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporation. Council President, Council Members, and City staff, thank you for the opportunity to speak this evening. I am here on behalf of the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporations and the families we serve. We appreciate the city and Buc-ee’s for conducting an initial traffic study and for sharing the updated remote this last week. We're not opposed to the development. However, we do have significant concerns about what the updated study demonstrates and the limited scope of the proposed mitigations. Our responsibility is to ensure that any changes along Worthsville Road support safe, reliable operations for our students, families, and our bus drivers. The updated Buc-ee’s traffic study provides new data on projected traffic volumes and interception performance during school drop-off and pickup windows. Although the city concludes that the site “does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school- related peak periods,” several findings, including our own observations, indicate meaningful concerns for school operations and student safety. First, school peak traffic is already operating at a near rush-hour intensity. PM drop-off volumes are only about 50 vehicles lower than evening rush-hour peak. Because these peaks do not overlap, Buc-ee’s traffic represents additional load, not shared load. Second, the multiple intersections show significant delay growth between current conditions and 2037 projections. Worthsville and Emerson (northbound) shows substantial increases in delay in the report. Worthsville and Southlake (southbound) already experiences significant drop-off delays and it's projected to nearly double. Worthsville Road and County Road 200 shows delays exceeding 120 seconds or two minutes today- both AM southbound and PM northbound with worsening delays projected. These are the same intersections that our buses and our student drivers and our families use in order to get to the middle school and the two elementary schools there. Third Buc-ee’s is projected to add 1,045 trips during the morning drop-off and 1,380 trips during afternoon pickup. The study attempts to differentiate where these trips go afterwards, but the impact occurs the moment we enter the roadway, Worthsville Road. During compressed school windows, any added volume destabilizes flow. Fourth, only one mitigation has been proposed, re-striving at the southbound approach at Worthsville Road and Ray Crowe Way. And this is the entrance to the middle school. No other improvements have been recommended for intersections already showing severe delays. If striking Ray Crowe Way was the solution, we would have thought about it and would have done it before now. Finally, despite these findings, the study concludes that Buc-ee's does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school-related periods. This conclusion does not align with the data that was presented or with school-specific traffic behavior. Because of these concerns, the district respectfully requests a formal commitment from the city and Buc-ee’s. If Buc-ee's operations create significant negative impact on our instructional day, bus routing our on-time performance, or parent pickup and drop-off operations, we just asking that the city and Buc-ee’s re-engage with us collaboratively to identify and implement mitigation strategies, including additional studies or infrastructure improvements. There's very little we can do on our own without more help. Our focus is simple: to ensure that the daily experience of our students, families, and staff remains safe and predictable as this progress progresses. We value our partnership with the city and Buc- ee’s and we want to continue to work together constructively. Thank you for your time and attention. Tim Edsell, Clark-Pleasant School Superintendent Appreciate your leadership. Again, I appreciate a couple of you who met with me individually. Appreciate you listening. I appreciate Scott Ratcliffe, who is one of the senior engineers for Buc-ee’s, for producing the revised traffic study. To me and to us as a school corporation last week. I appreciate them willing to redo the traffic study that last week of August. President Crawford just said a lot of similar points. I'll reiterate a few of them, but not to be repetitive and for the sake of brevity. I do want to emphasize some of those key areas that are of concern to us with the traffic flow That would be Worthsville & Emerson, Worthsville & South Lake Avenue, and Worthsville & County Rd 200 The one suggestion to obviously reach strike the left and turn lanes that's on our property right by middle school entrance. Appreciate that. We could do that. Signage, we could do that. My final request would be: as Buc-ee’s is built, I would love to see improved and stronger communication from all entities because, as it's built and even as it opens up, whatever that timeframe is, and the impact that it will have on our school day is so significant. I would love to work together with, again, all entities because it's important that obviously we conduct school. I've made our Department of Education aware of this. And so, the goal is for us, to work with you, not to be against you, but to make sure that we have school every single day within the required hours that were allotted. Thank you for your time. Mitch Hunter, 3114 East 700 North in Whiteland, Indiana, 46184. Updating the comprehensive plan involves not only community input, hiring the third-party companies of HWC Engineering and Stantec. The project siphoned $200,000 from the city budget. The goal was for the final project to be “the blueprint for the future.” The land in question tonight falls in a major part of that blueprint, one the city deemed worthy of developing a specific vision for how the area will be used and what it would look like in the years to come (Greenwood Crossing). The plan says it is critical that this area holds a strong set of development criteria to ensure new development allows the city to grow its tax base, of course, but also to protect adjacent rural lifestyles. The new plan acknowledges Greenwood residents expressed their concern throughout the process about industrial development continuing south pass Worthsville Road. Additionally, the HWC Steering Committee held a meeting specifically addressing the future land use of this area. The very first bullet point meeting states: “Areas surrounding the I-65 and Worthsville Road interchange should remain largely residential with limited commercial uses that serve the surrounding neighborhoods and not those traveling along the highway.” There are two major issues regarding this land and its proposed use. First, the community repeatedly expressed its concern about industrial and warehouse development in the area. Similar projects in the area have not come to fruition because the city listened to the residents and honored their promise to prevent industrial developments. But it's important to note that the problem with proposed industrial developments in the past was not with the business of logistics itself. Rather, it is what those businesses bring to the land: massive structures, invasive lighting, and daunting amounts of traffic. Though not in the business of logistics, a Buc-ee’s brings all of those things front and center, industrial or not. Even though they themselves clearly thought that their operations warranted industrial classifications when they originally brought this before the APC. The spirit of no warehouses and no industrial was to guard against these types of developments. Secondly, allowing this development or any like it will destroy the vision for Greenwood Crossing. The plan calls for a development that is harmonious with residential development on adjacent properties. However, a 120-pump gas station is a poisoned pill. It spoils the land around it. Here is a visual of 37 Buc-ee’s across the United States.I emailed this to each of you earlier. Thank you for those that responded, confirming that you received it. What it shows here is there's a radius of 2,500 feet from the proposed site. The distance that in our plan is supposed to be residential. And when you look at that, you will see that there is no new housing development in any of those 37. Maybe some was existing, but nothing new. All that comes afterwards is warehouses and other large-scale development buildings. Every Buc-ee’s dead zone is a far cry from what Greenwood Crossing is supposed to be, from what we spent $200,000 to plan, and from what this Council promised was in our future. Thank You Mike Venatta, 1085 S Nay Rd, Greenwood, retired. We built our house 25 years ago on Nay Road. And I see several things with Buc-ee’s, and I'm not anti-Buc-ee’s. I'm anti-the location of this Buc-ee’s in Greenwood at this particular location. One, it really doesn't bring hundreds of pre-paying jobs. If you look at it close it brings jobs that are almost identical to the warehouse jobs that we've got now in Greenwood. Of the 200 jobs there, five of them would have enough money to buy a medium-sized house in the city of Greenwood. Again, I'm not putting down the job thing. What is important is, I think, what the last gentleman said quite a bit, and the confusion that's out there, if you look, I just got this letter today from INDOT, and it was something I've been requesting. And thank goodness they shared the traffic info with these other people first. But I'm going to read you, if you would, and if you trust an old guy that's 75 years old. What you see on the internet when you pull this up. Last Friday, I did an AI overview request on the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange looking for this new study. Here's what I got: the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange in Greenwood, Indiana, can handle roughly 23,000 vehicles per day, but traffic data shows it is already pushing its design limits. Daily capacity recent traffic impact studies and local projections highlight that the current volume of 23,000 vehicles daily already causes the interchange to approach or fail standard design levels during peak hours. The diverging diamond interchange, which Mayor Myers bragged about and should have years ago, about taking the load off the south side, keeping traffic moving smoothly. And remember, we have neighbors too, Whiteland, New Whiteland, that are building up like crazy. But it says this interchange is highly effective at moving traffic efficiently without requiring left turns. However, area growth from local schools, (God bless them), and residential developments has heavily burdened its capacity. Buc-ee’s impact: Travel projections show that adding an estimated 15,000 new daily trips on top of the existing 23,000 vehicles would cause the intersection flow to fail completely. And here's something I want to ask you guys to consider deeply. I'm old, I can watch YouTube, and I love watching that. Here's Indiana, here's the growing counties, here's the growing cities. Greenwood's been on there, and one of the major advantages of Greenwood is being close to Indianapolis. And not having congestion to get there. They have said repeatedly with Fishers and Carmel, I-69 is a mess every morning. So, I want you to consider this, if you would, please. Of the estimated daily vehicles, and this is the breakdown, I guess, the way that Buc-ee’s does it: pass by intercept: 10,500 to 12,000 is existing highway traffic pulling off and returning to I-65. No new cars added. Great. The next one: primary new trips, brand new trips generated to local roads explicitly to visit Buc-ee’s. Think Indianapolis, think Franklin, think Shelbyville, think Bloomington, think everywhere. I'm not a traffic analyst by any means. I'm college educated. I do have 40 years of corporate experience, but don't tell me that Greenwood isn't facing congestion now on holidays and weekends. And how do you explain adding up to 4,500 more cars every day from local roads? It's not going to just affect us on the south side, it's going to affect all of Greenwood. And just please consider that. And plus, I guess to sum up, there's 1,500 homes or residents that are going to be affected, probably lose five to ten percent of their value. Mine's one of them. But that's just me personally. But everyone in Greenwood is going to be affected by the congestion and the other things. So please consider that, thank you for your time. Carmen Madson, 121 South Meridian Street, Greenwood, IN. I am for Buc-ee’s, I have been to 3 states, 4 Buc-ee’s and have never had a problem getting in or out. I've been to one as an open, never had a problem getting in or out. I love Buc-ee’s. I love the food. I love the people. I love the merchandise. I think it would be good for Greenwood. As the back of my shirt says, life is better at Buc-ee’s. I would love to see that sign that says 240 miles to Buc-ee’s to say Greenwood, to Buc-ee’s, to Worthsville Avenue, your next Buc-ee’s. So please vote yes. We want Buc-ee’s. And that's hundreds of people on Facebook next door, Greenwood Chatter, Center Grove Chatter, who have tied in and said, bring it. So, bring it. Mike Campbell - That takes care of the 20 minutes on Ordinance 26-24. Anyone else here that would like to speak to the council concerning another item that is on tonight’s agenda? If so, please step to the podium and state your name and address. Seeing none and moving on V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider ORDINANCE NO. 26-24 AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND THE OFFICIAL ZONING MAP ADOPTED BY REFERENCE IN UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE NO. 20-29 (PROPOSED REZONING OF APPROXIMATELY 80.15 ACRES LOCATED ON THE SOUTHEAST CORNER OF I-65 AND WORTHSVILLE ROAD (Sponsors Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Lekse and Manship) Bryan Tuohy, 9294 North Meridian Street representing CSMS Management LLC, an affiliate of Buc-ee's LLC, presented the petition. He introduced members of the Buc-ee’s development team and outlined the proposed project on approximately 80 acres at the southeast corner of Worthsville Road and I-65. Mr. Tuohy stated the proposal is consistent with the City’s Comprehensive Plan designation of Regional Destination Commercial within the Greenwood Crossing area. He noted the development would include a 74,000-square-foot Buc-ee’s travel center, approximately 175 to 225 employees, an estimated $9 million annual payroll, and a capital investment of approximately $50 million. Mr. Tuohy reviewed the proposed site improvements, which include extensive landscaping, more than one mile of multi-use trails, sidewalks, and public open space. He also outlined developer-funded traffic improvements, including a roundabout at Worthsville Road and Collins Road/County Road 250 East, multiple access points to the site, additional turn lanes, a traffic signal at the main entrance, and extended storage lanes at the I-65 interchange ramps. The estimated cost of roadway improvements was stated to be between $13 million and $14 million. Mr. Tuohy summarized traffic studies completed in June and September 2026, stating that with the proposed improvements, surrounding intersections would adequately accommodate development traffic and that no significant impacts were identified during school-related peak periods. He noted Buc-ee’s committed to completing traffic improvements before opening the store. During Council discussion, Mr. Moan asked what percentage of Buc-ee’s customers are travelers rather than local residents. Scott Ratcliff, Director of Engineering for Buc-ee’s, responded that approximately 90 to 92 percent of retail transactions occur outside the local ZIP code and that a significant percentage of customers travel more than 100 miles to visit a location. Mr. Hill expressed concerns regarding Buc-ee’s involvement in intellectual property litigation and stated that those concerns would lead him to vote against the proposal. Ms. Gibson reported visiting the Buc-ee’s location in Huber Heights, Ohio. She stated she observed no significant traffic issues and shared positive feedback from employees regarding wages, benefits, scheduling flexibility, and workplace environment. Mr. Nelson, presented City staff's recommendation for approval of PC-2026-035. He stated that the Technical Review Committee provided a favorable recommendation, the Advisory Plan Commission voted 8-0 to recommend approval, and the proposal is generally consistent with the City's adopted plans and future land use policies. Mr. Nelson also requested a technical amendment to the PUD document to correct a missing value in Section 7.12.1 regarding building façade materials. The amendment specified that precast concrete panels may not exceed 80 percent of the front elevation. Mr. Hopper asked whether Buc-ee’s had information regarding the percentage of sales attributable to prepared food items. Mr. Ratcliff indicated he did not have that information available but agreed to provide it later. Mr. Campbell requested a motion to amend Ordinance No. 26-24 as recommended by Planning Director Mr. Nelson. Motion to amend Ord. No. 26-24 to insert 7.12.1 (1.) (d.) in any event pre-cast concrete panels should not exceed an area more than 80% of the front elevation. Motion by Lekse seconded by Hopper Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan, Hoggatt Motion passes: 9-0 Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-24 as amended by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan Nays – Hill, Hoggatt Motion passes: 7-2 B. items.title: ORDINANCE NO. 26-40 AN ORDINANCE AMENDING GREENWOOD MUNICIPAL CODE (1993), AS AMENDED, TO ADOPT A NEW ARTICLE 10 USE OF MOTORIZED SCOOTERS AND ARTICLE 11 REGULATION OF ELECTRIC BICYCLES WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD.
items.text: Page 1 of 13 GREENWOOD COMMON COUNCIL ORDINANCE NO. 26-40 AN ORDINANCE AMENDING GREENWOOD MUNICIPAL CODE (1993), AS AMENDED, TO ADOPT A NEW ARTICLE 10 USE OF MOTORIZED SCOOTERS AND ARTICLE 11 REGULATION OF ELECTRIC BICYCLES WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD. WHEREAS, the City of Greenwood has the authority to adopt ordinances regulating parking on the streets and public rights -of-way within its jurisdiction pursuant to Ind. Code § 9 - 21-1-2 and 3; WHEREAS, Indiana Code §36-9-6-2 authorizes the Board of Public Works and Safety to supervise the streets, alleys, public grounds, and other property of the City; WHEREAS, Indiana Code §36-9-6-3 authorizes the Board of Public Works and Safety to have custody of and maintain all real and personal property of the City; WHEREAS, the legislative body of the City (“Council”) is responsible for determining ordinance violations and penalties for violations including, without limitation, violations of the traffic code; WHEREAS, the use of electric scooters, electric bicycles and o ther similar devices has increased substantially, offering a convenient, environmentally conscious, and affordable mode of transportation; and WHEREAS, it is essential to establish clear regulations governing the operation of electric scooters, electric bicycles and other devices to ensure the safety of riders, pedestrians, and other users of City’s sidewalks, trails, and roadways, and to promote sustainable transportation options while managing potential conflicts, minimizing risks to riders, pedestrians, and congestion; and WHEREAS, these regulations are intended to complement and not supersede existing state and federal laws pertaining to the operation of motor vehicles and other transportation devices. WHEREAS, the Council now desires to adopt this ordinance establishing certain provisions of Chapter 8, Article10. Regulation of Motorized Scooters and Article 11. Regulations of Electric Bicycles of the City of Greenwood Municipal Code. NOW THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED BY THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA, THAT: Section 1. Greenwood Municipal Code (1993), Chapter 8, Traffic and Parking Regulations is hereby amended to insert a new article, Article 10. Regulation of Motorized Scooters to read as follows: Sec. 8-101 Definitions. Shared-use motorized scooter means a conveyance or device propelled by a motor, not having a seat or saddle for the use of the rider, with two or more wheels in contact with the ground, with a floorboard for the user to stand upon, and that is held out for rent, lease, or otherwise ma de available for use by members of the public through a Shared-use Mobility System. The term does not include the following: (1) A device used to aid a person with a disability, including but not limited to a motorized wheelchair. (2) A non-shared-use bicycle, whether said bicycle is motorized or not. Motorized scooter means a conveyance or device propelled by a motor, not having a seat or saddle for the use of the rider, with two or more wheels in contact with the ground, and with a floorboard for the user to stand upon. The term does not include the following: Ord. No. 26-40 Page 2 of 13 (1) A device used to aid a person with a disability, including but not limited to a motorized wheelchair. (2) A bicycle, whether said bicycle is motorized or not. Shared-use Bicycle means a conveyance or device whether propelled by a motor or not, having a seat or saddle for the use of the rider, with two or more wheels in contact with the ground, and that is held out for rent, lease, or otherwise made available for use by members of the public through a Shared-use Mobility System. Shared-use Mobility System means a system comprised of a number of shared -use mobility devices of one or many types as described in this Section, which are provided to Users for short term rentals for point-to-point trips; and which may be locked or unlocked for use with or without being located on a rack or docking system. User means a person who rents and uses from an Operator, or allows another person to use an Operator’s shared-use mobility device. Multi-Use Trail A paved or unpaved path designated for use by pedestrians, bicyclists, and, with the exception of disability assistive devices, other non-motorized modes of travel. Park Trail A paved or unpaved path designated for use by pedestrians, bicyclists, and, with the exception of disability assistive devices, other non -motorized modes of travel operated or maintained by the City of Greenwood Parks and Recreation Board or Department. Operator means a person or entity that operates, owns, manages, or otherwise controls a Shared- Use mobility System. Public right-of-way means any publicly travelled way or any public easement. Shared-use path means any paved pathway in the public right-of-way which is at least eight feet wide. Sidewalk means any paved walkway less than eight feet wide between the curb lines of a street, or the lateral lines of a roadway, and the adjacent property lines intended for the use of pedestrians. Street. Any public roadway within the City limits which is primarily used for purposes of vehicular travel. Sec. 8-102 Applicability of state laws. Every person who operates a motorized scooter, whether said motorized scooter is a shared -use motorized scooter or not, or a shared -use Bicycle upon any street, road, trail, path, or sidewalk shall be subject to state law concerning such conveyance. Every person who operates a motorized scooter or shared-use Bicycle shall also be subject to all city ordinances except where the nature of shared-use bicycles or motorized scooters renders said ordinances inapplicable to either. Sec. 8-103. License required; fee. (a) It shall be unlawful to operate a Shared -use Mobility System without first obtaining a license from the Board of Public Works and Safety. (b) Each Shared-use Mobility System operator shall pay license fees as established by the Board of Public Works. License fees may be updated from time -to-time by the Board of Public Works in order to properly reflect the City's expenses associated with allowin g shared -use motorized scooters in the public right-of-way. (c) Licenses shall expire one year after issuance. In order to continue operating, a Shared -use Mobility System operator shall apply for a new license at least thirty (30) days prior to the expiration of its existing license. The Board of Public Works shall es tablish fees for renewal licenses, which may or may not be the same as the fees set forth for first-time licensees. Ord. No. 26-40 Page 3 of 13 (d) An application for a Shared-use Mobility System license shall be made on a form provided by the Board of Public Works, shall be signed by an authorized representative of the Shared-use Mobility System operator, and shall include, at a minimum, the following information: (1) The maximum number of shared -use motorized scooters or shared-use bicycles the Shared-use Mobility System operator may deploy within the corporate boundaries of the City during the applicable license term; (2) A description of all shared -use motorized scooters or shared-use bicycles that will be deployed, including the model, manufacturer, and color of each shared-use motorized scooter or shared-use bicycle; (3) Color photographs depicting the shared -use motorized scooter(s) or shared -use bicycles; (4) A schedule of rates and charges that the applicant will charge to users; (5) Detailed staffing and operational plans, including information regarding (i) local staffing and (ii) contractors the Shared-use Mobility System operator will utilize to perform services related to its Shared-use Mobility System; (6) A GPS or GIS -based map depicting the proposed service area of the shared -use motorized scooters or shared-use bicycles; (7) A 24-hour customer service telephone number through which users and members of the public may contact the Shared-use Mobility System operator and that will be displayed on each shared-use motorized scooter; (8) A signed agreement indemnifying the City on a form provided by the Board of Public Works; (9) Proof of all insurance required by the Board of Public Works, including, if required, a bond; (10) A signed agreement stating that during a special event the City may prohibit devices from being located in or operated in those areas designated for the special event; and (11) Any other information deemed necessary by the Board of Public Works. (e) Upon receipt of a completed license application and any required supporting documentation, the Board of Public Works shall either issue or deny the application for a license during a public meeting. In making this determination, the Board of Public Works shall, among other factors, consider the extent to which the applicant's prior or ongoing operations have complied with the law. (f) A Shared-use Mobility System operator that has obtained a license shall be permitted to deploy, at a maximum, the number of shared -use motorized devices authorized by the Board of Public Works. During license renewal, the Board of Public Works may increase or decrease the number of shared-use mobility devices a Shared-use Mobility System operator is permitted to deploy. (g) Any Shared-use Mobility System operator that operates without first having obtained a license or violates any provision of this Section shall be subject to the penalties set forth within this Code, up to and including a fine of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500). Except for those violations which, by their very nature, can occur more than once in one day, each day that a violation continues shall constitute a s eparate violation. In addition, any Shared-use Mobility System operator that violates any provision in this Chapter or any other condition imposed by the Board of Public Works may be penalized with the revocation of the Shared-use Mobility System operator's license. (h) If the Board of Public Works denies an application submitted by a Shared-use Mobility Ord. No. 26-40 Page 4 of 13 System operator, the Board shall issue written findings indicating the reasons for said denial. Any Shared-use Mobility System operator that has had its application denied may appeal said denial to the Johnson County Circuit Court, provided that any such appeal is filed with the Court within thirty days of the Board issuing its written findings. Sec. 8-104 Restrictions on operation imposed by regulation. When issuing a license, the Board of Works and Safety may by regulation impose appropriate conditions on the operation of Shared Mobility Systems in order to further the purposes of this Section, including but not limited to, the following: (1) Limits on the locations in which a Shared Mobility System may operate; (2) Designations of the specific locations where Shared Mobility Devices or docking stations may be stored or parked when not in use; (3) Limits on the number of Shared Mobility Devices permitted in the Shared Mobility System; (4) Standards for the use and maintenance of Shared Mobility Devices; (5) Restriction on the use of any motorized device on any shared -use path, Park trail, or multi-use trail; (6) Other regulations necessary to further the purposes of this Chapter. Sec. 8-105 Indemnification, insurance. (a) Any Shared Mobility Device operator issued a license under this chapter shall, as a condition of the issuance and continued validity of the license to operate a Shared Mobility System, indemnify, hold harmless and defend, by counsel of the city’s choosing, the City and its respective officers, agents, officials and employees from any and all third party claims, actions, causes of action, judgments and liens to the extent they arise out of any negligent or wrongful act or omission, or violation of any provision of this Code or other law by an Operator or any of its officers, agents, employees and users arising from the operation, maintenance, or use of the shared mobility system and the Operator’s shared mobility devices. Such indemnity shall include attorneys’ fees and all costs and other expenses arising therefrom or incurred in connection therewith and shall not be limited by any insurance coverage required by this chapter or otherwise carried by the Operator. This indemnification requirement shall be memorialized in an agreement signed by an authorized representative of the Operator who is an officer or employee of the Operator with authority to legally bind the Operator, and the Operator shall be required to post an indemnity bond in favor of the city. Such agreement and indemnity bond shall be in a form approved by the City’s corporation counsel. (b) Any Shared Mobility Device Operator issued a license under this chapter shall, as a condition of the issuance and continued validity of the license to operate a shared mobility system, purchase and maintain a policy of commercial general liability insurance that will protect it and the City from claims for damages because of bodily injury and personal injury, including death and claims of damages to property which may arise out of or result from the operation, maintenance, or use of the shared mobility system and the operator’s shared mobility devices. (c) The commercial general liability insurance required under this subsection (e)(2) shall be not less than: (1) each occurrence limit of $1,000,000.00; (2) $100,000.00 for damage to rented premises; (3) $5,000.00 for medical expenses; (4) $500,000.00 for personal and advertising injury; (5) $1,000.000,00 products/completed operations; (6) $1,000,000.00 auto liability; (7) $2,000,000.00 general aggregate limit; (8) $5,000,000.00 excess/umbrella liability. Certificates of insurance naming the City as an additional insured showing such coverage then in force, but not less than the above amounts, shall be submitted by the Operator with its application for a license under this chapter. Such certificates shall contain a provision that the policies and coverage afforded thereunder will not be canceled until at least 30 days after written notice to the license administrator. Ord. No. 26-40 Page 5 of 13 (d) The failure to maintain the bond or insurance policies required under this Section throughout the entire term of a license shall constitute a violation of this Code. Sec. 8-106 License Revocation. (a) The Board of Public Works may revoke a Shared-use Mobility System operator's license at any time if it finds that one of the following conditions exists: (1) The Shared-use Mobility System operator has failed to comply with the requirements of this Chapter, including, but not limited to, requirements regarding parking, age of users, scooter condition, scooter equipment, scooter appearance, maintenance, lock-down, removal, data reporting, public outreach, or affordability and accessibility. (2) The Shared-use Mobility System operator has failed to comply with other reasonable requirements imposed by the Board of Public Works. (3) The Shared-use Mobility System operator has violated any federal law including, but not limited to, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) or federal regulation; any state law or regulation; or any local law or regulation. (b) Before the Board of Public Works revokes a Shared-use Mobility System operator's license under this Section, it shall conduct a hearing to consider the evidence supporting said revocation. Following the hearing, the Board shall issue written findings of fact. The Board's decision may be appealed to a court of competent jurisdiction, provided that any such appeal is filed with the Court within thirty ( 3 0 ) days of the Board issuing its decision. Sec. 8 -107 Shared-use motorized devices equipment, safety, condition, appearance, and hours of deployment. (a) All shared -use motorized scooters and shared -use bicycles shall be compliant with all applicable American National Standards Institute (ANSI), ASTM International, and Consumer Product Safety Commission standards. If additional organizations similar to those listed in this subsection establish standards applicable to shared-use motorized scooters, the board of public works may require that all shared-use bicycles and motorized scooters comply with said additional standards. (b) All shared -use bicycles and shared-use motorized scooters shall be equipped so as to operate at a speed no greater than fifteen miles per hour. (c) All shared -use motorized scooters and shared -use bicycles shall be assigned a unique identification number. The unique identification number must be visible to the user and to nearby pedestrians and must also identify the shared -use motorized scooter operator shared-use bicycle operator. (d) All shared-use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle system operators shall display the following items conspicuously on each shared-use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle: (1) The required twenty-four-hour telephone number at which members of the public may contact the shared-use motorized scooter operator; (2) The shared-use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle operator's website; (3) Mobile application information of the shared -use motorized scooter and shared -use bicycle operator; (4) That users are encouraged to wear helmets; (5) That users are required to obey all traffic laws; (6) That users shall yield to pedestrians in the right-of-way; and Ord. No. 26-40 Page 6 of 13 (7) That users must follow proper parking procedures. (e) All shared-use motorized scooters and shared-use bicycles shall be further equipped with the following: (1) A lamp on the front exhibiting a white light visible from a distance of at least five hundred feet to the front; (2) a bell, horn, or other lawful signaling device. (3) A lamp on the rear exhibiting a red light visible from a distance of at least five hundred feet to the rear or a red reflector visible from a distance of at least five hundred feet to the rear; and (4) A brake enabling a person who operates a shared-use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle to make the braked wheels skid on dry, level, clean pavement. (f) All shared -use motorized scooters and shared -use bicycles shall be capable of being remotely locked down by the shared-use system operator upon any report that the shared -use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle is not operating properly, pending a proper evaluation. (g) All shared -use motorized scooters and shared -use bicycles shall be maintained in a reasonably clean condition and proper working condition. (h) All shared-use motorized scooters and shared-use bicycles must meet any and all additional standards required by the Board of Public Works and Safety. (i) Any shared-use motorized scooter and shared -use bicycle system operator that deploys either in violation of this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth the City of Greenwood Municipal Code. Sec. 8-108 Parking. (a) Except as indicated herein, this section applies to any motorized scooter, whether or not the motorized scooter is a shared-use motorized scooter. (b) Motorized scooters may be parked at any bicycle parking facility located in the public right-of-way. (c) Motorized scooter parking is permitted on sidewalks, share-use paths, and multi-use trails with the following limitations: (1) Motorized scooters shall be parked in an upright position. (2) Motorized scooters shall be parked so as to leave a clear straight pathway at least fifty- four inches wide, and such clear pathway shall be measured from the widest part of the path. The fifty-four inches shall not include the width of the curb. (3) Under no circumstance shall motorized scooters be parked so as to obstruct: i. Any parking space, including any parking access aisle; ii. Any loading zone; iii. Any curb ramp; iv. Any public transportation infrastructure including, but not limited to, bus shelters, bus stop signs, or passenger waiting areas; v. Any driveway; vi. Any entrance or exit from any building; vii. Any fire hydrant, emergency call box, or other emergency facility; viii. Any parking meter; ix. Any utility pole or utility box; x. Any street furniture or news rack; xi. Any commercial window display; or xii. A crosswalk button. Ord. No. 26-40 Page 7 of 13 (d) Motorized scooters may be parked by riders on unimproved surfaces when no more than two are placed parallel to the street and touching a city traffic or parking sign located in a tree plot or grassy zone, without plantings such as flowers or ornamental grass, between a sidewalk and the street. (e) Under no circumstance shall motorized scooters be parked so as to impede accessibility under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), so as to impede access to accessible parking zones, or so as to impede access to parking spaces designated for persons with disabilities. (f) No person shall park a shared-use motorized scooter within the designated boundaries of a special event for which a special event permit has been obtained. (g) Motorized scooters shall not be parked upon any street or alley. (h) Except as permitted by subparts (b), (c), (d) of this Section, motorized scooters shall not be parked upon any public property. (i) In order to verify compliance with the requirements of this section, shared -use motorized scooter operators and shared-use bicycle operators shall require shared-use motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle users to take a photograph demonstrating the location of their parked scooter or bicycle at the conclusion of their rental. (j) The city may move any shared -use motorized scooter that is parked in violation of this section to a location where the scooter may be lawfully parked. If the city opts to move an illegally parked shared-use motorized scooter to a legal parking position, th e city may nonetheless assess any applicable fines in accordance with this chapter. (k) A shared-use bicycle shall be parked at a bicycle rack or a docking station and shall be parked in an upright manner. Shared-use bicycles shall not be parked in any other manner or area other than provided in this subsection. (l) Any shared-use motorized scooter or shared-use bicycle parked in violation of this section or located so as to pose a hazard to public health and safety may be immediately removed and impounded by the City. (b) Motorized scooters shall not be permitted on any sidewalk, shared-use path, Park trail, or multi-use trail when the motorized scooter exceeds 15 miles per hour when the battery or electric motor assisted propulsion function is engaged. (c) Shared-use bicycles shall not be permitted on any sidewalk, shared-use path, Park trail, or multi-use trail when the shared-use bicycle exceeds 15 miles per hour when the battery or electric motor assisted propulsion function is engaged. (d) Every person riding a motorized scooter or shared use bicycle upon a street shall be granted all of the rights and shall be subject to all of the duties applicable to the driver of a vehicle. (e) Every person riding a motorized scooter and shared-use bicycles upon a sidewalk shall be granted all of the rights and shall be subject to all of the duties applicable to a pedestrian. (f) The regulations in the traffic code applicable to motorized Scooters and shared-use bicycles shall apply whenever a either is operated upon any roadway or public sidewalk or upon any shared- use path, subject to those exceptions stated herein. (g) The operator of a motorized scooter and shared-use bicycle shall not overtake standing vehicles in a travel lane. Ord. No. 26-40 Page 8 of 13 (h) A User operating a motorized scooter or a battery assisted shared-use bicycle on a sidewalk, shared-use path, Park trail, multi-use trail, or within a crosswalk shall yield the right-of-way to any pedestrian. (i) A User who is operating a motorized scooter or shared-use bicycle and who is passing a pedestrian traveling on the same sidewalk, shared-use path, Park trail, multi-use trail, or within a crosswalk shall pass the pedestrian at a distance of at least three feet. If the User is operating the motorized scooter or a shared-use bicycle is unable to pass the pedestrian at a distance of at least three feet, then the User shall stop, dismount, or exit the sidewalk, shared-use path, Park trail, multi-use trail, or within a crosswalk. Agenda Amendment - Ordinance No. 26-40 A motion was made by Ms. Gibson to add Ordinance No. 26-40 to the agenda. The motion was seconded by Ms. Kasch. The presiding officer asked if there were any questions regarding the request. Hearing none, a vote was taken. The motion passed by voice vote, Ordinance No. 26-40 was added to the agenda and scheduled as the final item of business. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5- minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit Fire Chief Washel stated that over the past several weeks, the Mayor’s Office, Controller’s Office, Fire Department, and Fire Merit Commission members had worked collaboratively to improve firefighter pay and benefits. He explained that those efforts resulted in a forward-thinking, multi- year salary matrix plan designed to provide a clear roadmap for future compensation. Chief Washel stated that the plan establishes direction and clarity, provides predictability and flexibility, and creates a sustainable framework for long-term success. He noted that the plan would enhance departmental stability, strengthen recruitment and retention efforts, and address both current and future departmental needs through a structured and intentional approach. Chief Washel emphasized that the plan was the result of a collaborative effort among department members, Fire Merit Commission members, executive staff, and the Mayor’s Administration. He thanked the Merit Commission members, Controller Greg Wright, Deputy Mayor Terry McLaughlin, and Mayor Mark Myers for their leadership, support, and contributions. He specifically recognized Mayor Myers for his vision and commitment to investing in the Greenwood Fire Department. Chief Washel stated that he fully supported the proposed Fire Department budget, noting that it reflected responsible planning, support for firefighters, and a sustainable path forward for the department. He concluded by urging the Council to support the budget. Brent Rockwell, District Vice President of Local 4252 and the District Vice President of Greenwood addressed the Council on behalf of the union membership. He referenced concerns previously raised regarding firefighter retention, pension competitiveness, and retirement benefits, noting that five full-time firefighters had departed for other departments during the past year. Mr. Rockwell stated that union representatives, through the Meet and Confer process, worked collaboratively with Fire Department leadership and City administration to develop a proposed multi-year pay matrix aimed at strengthening compensation, improving the pension base, and enhancing recruitment and retention efforts. He stated that discussions among all parties had been positive and constructive and expressed hope that the pay matrix would help retain trained personnel and support continued high-quality service to Greenwood residents. Mr. Rockwell concluded by thanking the Meet and Confer team, the Greenwood Common Council, Fire Chief Jamie Washel, City Controller Greg Wright, Deputy Mayor Terry McLaughlin, and Mayor Mark Myers for their collaboration and support. Mr. Campbell commented that it was refreshing to see all parties working collaboratively and aligned on the matter under discussion. V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider B. Mr. Moan indicated he was uncertain of the specific details of the project but noted that Ms. Wolfe expressed concern that the company could not commit to reaching the 160-job target in the foreseeable future. Motion to pass second reading Res. No. 26-10 by Hopper, seconded by Lekse Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan Motion passes: 8-0 VI. New Business – Introductions of New Ordinances and Resolutions ORDINANCE NO. 26-37 AN ORDINANCE VACATING PLATTED FIFTEENFOOT DRAINAGE AND UTILITY EASEMENT IN BLOCK C OF THE REPLAT OF THE REPLAT OF BLOCK B, GREENBROOKE PARKE PUBLIC HEARING scheduled for November 4, 2026 (Sponsor Lekse) ORDINANCE NO. 26-38 AN ORDINANCE VACATING PLATTED TWENTY- FOOT DRAINAGE AND UTILITY EASEMENT IN LOT 2 OF THE SUBPLAT FOR GREENWOOD AIR PARK BLOCK 5 PUBLIC HEARING scheduled for November 4, 2026 (Sponsor Lekse) ORDINANCE NO. 26-39 AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE 2026 SALARY ORDINANCE, COMMON COUNCIL ORDINANCE NO. 25-20, TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF CAPTAIN, LIEUTENANT, AND ENGINEER FIRE DEPARTMENT (Sponsor Moan) Motion to suspend the rules Ord. No. 26-39 through first reading by Kasch, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Gibson, Hill, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan, Campbell Motion passes: 8-0 Motion to pass first reading Ord. No. 26-39 by Lekse, seconded by Kasch Votes: Ayes - Hill, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Motion passes: 8-0 Motion to suspend the rules Ord. No. 26-39 through second reading by Kasch seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill Motion Passes: 8-0 RESOLUTION NO. 26-11 A RESOLUTION ESTABLISHING HOLIDAYS FOR EMPLOYEES OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsor Campbell) ORDINANCE NO. 26-40 AN ORDINANCE AMENDING GREENWOOD MUNICIPAL CODE (1993), AS AMENDED, TO ADOPT A NEW ARTICLE 10 USE OF MOTORIZED SCOOTERS AND ARTICLE 11 REGULATION OF ELECTRIC BICYCLES WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD (Sponsor Hopper) Chief Ison addressed the Council regarding Ordinance No. 26-40. He stated that the Police Department had worked with legal counsel for approximately one month to develop the proposed regulations after becoming aware of a shared mobility scooter business operating within the city. Chief Ison explained that the scooters are rented through smartphone applications and are often left on sidewalks, public property, parking lots, streets, and private property. Chief Ison noted concerns regarding public safety, including hazards to both riders and pedestrians using sidewalks and trailways. He stated that the ordinance was designed to regulate not only shared mobility scooters but also electric bicycles, which have become increasingly popular. The proposed regulations include provisions addressing operating speeds, the safe overtaking of pedestrians, and other safety measures intended to protect residents. In response to a question from Mr. Moan, Chief Ison confirmed that, without a local ordinance, only state traffic laws govern the operation of such devices. He explained that additional local regulations are needed to address their use on city trailways and sidewalks, as well as business operations and the placement of devices within the city. VII. Miscellaneous Business A. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters not on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit. Randy Goodin, 1157 Central Park Blvd., Greenwood, Indiana, stated that he had been in discussions with members of the Lions Club regarding the establishment of a Greenwood Lions Club. He introduced representatives of the organization to provide information about their mission and community service efforts. Nancy Baxter, 9005 Robey Drive, Indianapolis, Indiana, spoke in support of forming a Lions Club in Greenwood. She explained that Lions Clubs International is one of the world's oldest service organizations, with clubs operating in numerous countries. Ms. Baxter described the organization's commitment to assisting communities and noted that Lions members had previously partnered with a Greenwood business owner to provide assistance following a disaster. She stated that similar community service projects could benefit Greenwood residents. Reed Fish, 8344 West 21st Street, Indianapolis, Indiana, addressed the Council regarding the Lions Club's service mission. He explained that Lions Clubs work alongside organizations such as Rotary and Kiwanis to support local communities through volunteer service and charitable projects. Mr. Fish noted that his local Lions Club had directed significant fundraising proceeds toward supporting parks, public safety agencies, and schools. He also provided an example of a Lions Club assuming responsibility for the operation and maintenance of a community park when local resources were limited. Mr. Fish stated that the group hoped to establish a Greenwood Lions Club and requested the Council's assistance in identifying community members who may be interested in participating. He encouraged support for the organization's efforts and offered informational materials regarding membership and the Lions Club mission. The Council thanked the speakers for their presentation. B. Council A. Other Miscellaneous B. Corporation Counsel C. Controller D. Mayor VIII. Adjournment 7:32 pm ______________________ ______________________ Mike Campbell, President Jeannine Myers, Clerk

Community Development Block Grants
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) provides resources to help Greenwood maintain decent housing, suitable living environments, and expand economic opportunity for low- and moderate-income citizens. Greenwood may only use CDBG to fund activities serving Greenwood residents.
Public Input Requested: Program Year 2026 Action Plan
Greenwood will receive $297,789 in Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) for the 2026 Program Year (PY2026) running October 1, 2026 - September 30, 2027. The City invites residents, neighborhood groups, social service agencies, business community members, and interested citizens to participate in the development of the Action Plan.
CDBG Program Year 2026 Action Plan
How can you provide feedback?
1. Attend Public Hearing 2 on June 17, 2026, 6:30 PM
Greenwood Public Library, Community Room A, 310 South Meridian Street
Greenwood CDBG will present the projects, types of activities, and funding for the 2026 Program Year.
2. Provide a Public Comment June 18 - July 18, 2026
Greenwood will post the PY2026 Action Plan for review and public comments on this website and at the reference desk in the Greenwood Public Library. Commenters must include their name and ensure Greenwood receives comments by 5:00 PM on July 18, 2026. Greenwood will consider all formal public comments on the Action Plan before submitting the document and comments to HUD by August 14, 2026.
To submit a public comment, for further information, or to request an accommodation, please contact Kevin Steinmetz at cdbg@greenwood.in.gov , 317-887-5000 , or 300 South Madison Avenue, Greenwood, IN 46142. Please submit accommodation requests three business days in advance.
Stay Informed
To get citizen input on actions to accomplish the goals of this program, Greenwood collects community data, holds public hearings and solicits comments from residents . If you would like to be added to an email list to receive updates about the program, please email: CDBG@greenwood.in.gov .

Mayor Myers Highlights Growth, Opportunities and Priorities at 2026 State of the City
Mayor Outlines City Achievements and Four Key Pillars that Guide Greenwood’s Future
Today, Greenwood Mayor Mark W. Myers delivered his fifteenth annual State of the City to more than 250 business professionals, community members and residents at the Greenwood Fieldhouse. Hosted by Aspire Economic Development + Chamber Alliance and moderated by Eric Prime of Van Valer Law Firm, the discussion centered on the city’s continued growth, its recent achievements and the priorities that will guide Greenwood through 2026 and beyond.
Mayor Myers framed the conversation around four pillars: public safety, infrastructure, quality of life and economic development – emphasizing how each plays a role in Greenwood’s continued success. While celebrating the city’s momentum, the Mayor also acknowledged challenges facing communities statewide, including the impacts of SEA 1, the recent property tax legislation.
“I’m excited about the growth and opportunities Greenwood has ahead in 2026,” said Mayor Myers. “Like any community, we may face challenges, but we are ready to meet them head on and continue building on the good work happening across our city. Greenwood’s success comes from the people who live, work and invest here.”
During the event, Mayor Myers highlighted major public safety investments, including expanded staffing within the Greenwood Fire Department and Greenwood Police Department, and continued training initiatives and progress on Fire Station 95, which will improve emergency response times and regional training opportunities.
Infrastructure remains a key focus, with Mayor Myers outlining recent road improvements, traffic enhancements and stormwater projects. He also discussed Greenwood’s continued use of state and federal funding, grants and partnerships to maximize the impact of infrastructure investments while planning responsibly for future needs.
The Mayor highlighted quality-of-life initiatives that continue to shape daily life in Greenwood, including parks programming, recreation amenities, community events and placemaking efforts. Greenwood’s recognition by U.S. News & World Report as one of the best places to live and retire reflects the city’s ongoing focus on a strong live, work and play balance.
Mayor Myers celebrated economic development successes, including 21 new businesses, continued job creation and investment throughout Greenwood. He also highlighted the first full year of operation at Greenwood Sports Park, which welcomed more than 70,000 visitors and generated over $218,000 in revenue.
The State of the City serves as an opportunity to recognize the work of city employees, partners and community members while outlining a clear vision for the year ahead.

During the winter weather season, warming centers are available across Indiana to provide a safe, warm place for individuals in need. Indiana 211 offers the most up-to-date information on warming center locations and hours in your community.
Call: Speak directly with a Community Navigator. Phone: Dial 2-1-1 or 1-866-211-9966 Available Monday - Friday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Text: Get a list of warming centers near you. Text your ZIP Code to 898-211 Available Monday - Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Online Search: Find warming centers through the Indiana 211 resource database at IN211.org .
To report a new warming center or update an existing listing, contact Indiana 211’s resource team by email at in211database@fssa.in.gov .

items.text: Beech Grove City SchoolsPlan estratégico 2025 Compromiso y comunicación con la comunidad: Fortalecer las asociaciones y asegurar que cada voz sea escuchada Bienestar y pertenencia: Crear espacios seguros y acogedores donde todos los estudiantes, familias y personal se sientan valorados y apoyados Enseñanza y aprendizaje: Ofrecer oportunidades educativas atractivas y de alta calidad que garanticen que todos los estudiantes tengan el apoyo y el acceso que necesitan para tener éxito Desarrollo de liderazgo: Invertir en nuestros educadores y personal para formar líderes fuertes en todos los niveles. A través de la innovación, la colaboración y un profundo compromiso con la excelencia, este plan transformará las Escuelas de la Ciudad de Beech Grove, asegurando que nuestros estudiantes, personal y familias se sientan conectados, apoyados y preparados para el éxito de por vida. Estamos profundamente agradecidos por las voces, ideas y compromisos que han dado forma a este plan. Juntos, no solo estamos imaginando un futuro más brillante, sino que lo estamos construyendo activamente, asegurando que cada estudiante tenga la confianza, las oportunidades y el apoyo para prosperar. El trabajo que tenemos por delante es transformador, y nos sentimos honrados de embarcarnos en este viaje con nuestra comunidad. Con gratitud y determinación, Es con gran orgullo que compartimos el Plan Estratégico de las Escuelas de la Ciudad de Beech Grove, una hoja de ruta para nuestros estudiantes, personal y comunidad. Este plan refleja las voces de casi 2,000 partes interesadas que participaron en encuestas y grupos focales, junto con la dedicación de nuestro Comité Directivo, que incluyó a maestros, líderes, padres y miembros de la comunidad. Trabajando juntos, podemos afirmar con confianza que este plan se alinea con los valores y aspiraciones de Beech Grove. En el corazón de este plan se encuentra nuestro firme compromiso con el éxito de los estudiantes, guiados por nuestra visión, misión, valores fundamentales y creencias. Imaginamos las Escuelas de la Ciudad de Beech Grove como un lugar donde todos los estudiantes creen que la educación es la forma de cambiar el mundo, y a través de este plan, nos aseguraremos de que cada estudiante en Beech Grove tenga las oportunidades, el apoyo y las experiencias necesarias para prosperar. items.title: Download the Plan (English)
items.text: Beech Grove City SchoolsStrategic Plan 2025 Community Engagement and Communication – Strengthening partnerships and ensuring every voice is heard Wellness and Belonging – Creating safe and welcoming spaces where all students, families, and staff feel valued and supported Teaching and Learning – Delivering engaging, high-quality educational opportunities that ensure all students have the support and access they need to succeed Leadership Development – Investing in our educators and staff to grow strong leaders at every level. Through innovation, collaboration, and a deep commitment to excellence, this plan will transform Beech Grove City Schools—ensuring that our students, staff, and families feel connected, supported, and prepared for lifelong success. We are deeply grateful for the voices, ideas, and commitments that have shaped this plan. Together, we are not just envisioning a brighter future—we are actively building it, ensuring that every student has the confidence, opportunities, and support to thrive. The work ahead is transformative, and we are honored to embark on this journey with our community. With gratitude and determination, It is with great pride that we share the Beech Grove City Schools Strategic Plan, a roadmap for our students, staff, and community. This plan reflects the voices of nearly 2,000 stakeholders who participated in surveys and focus groups, along with the dedication of our Steering Committee, which included teachers, leaders, parents, and community members. Working together, we can confidently assert that this plan aligns with the values and aspirations of Beech Grove. At the heart of this plan is our fierce commitment to student success, guided by our vision, mission, core values, and beliefs. We envision Beech Grove City Schools to be a place where all students believe that education is the way to change the world, and through this plan, we will ensure every student in Beech Grove has the opportunities, support, and experiences needed to thrive. Our strategic goals are centered around four key areas: Dear Hornet Family, Dr. Laura Hammack, Superintendent of Beech Grove City Schools 5 Schools. 1 Family.In our schools, you’ll hear us talk about family and being stronger and better together. We are known for putting ‘we before me.’ Words matter and we use them with care. #Together #WeBeforeMe Vision Mission Beech Grove City Schools – where all students believe education is the way to change their world. We hold high expectations for every student by: 1) Delivering highly engaging educational opportunities 2) Designing individualized access, and 3) Developing student ownership for learning so every student is positioned for success the day they walk across the stage at graduation Values CommunityBelonging We create safe spaces where everyone feels welcomed, connected and valued. We place others above ourselves by serving and partnering with our community. We recognize and celebrate that our differences make us stronger

beech grove common council
The Beech Grove Common Council is comprised of seven members elected to four-year terms; two at-large and five elected from the five Council districts. The Council is the legislative body of the city. It adopts the annual budget for the city, appropriates tax monies, passes city ordinances and resolutions, and makes appointments to certain boards and commissions. Regular meetings of the Com mon Council are held at 7:00 p.m. on the first Monday of each month. In the event the regular meeting day falls on a legal holiday, the meeting will be held the day following the holiday. Special meetings may called by the Mayor with at least three days notice and for a specified purpose. The Mayor, or in his or her absence the President Pro-Tempore of the Common Council, serves as presiding officer. Email the entire council at citycouncil@beechgrove.com .

(Beech Grove, Ind.) Mechanical Skills, Inc. and the City of Beech Grove will celebrate the grand opening of a new plumbing apprenticeship training center on Monday, Aug. 10 , marking the completion of a project that has transformed a longtime vacant parcel into a hub for the skilled trades in the heart of the city.
Located at 1831 Albany Street, the site was once home to a Marsh and Safeway grocery store before sitting vacant for years. The new 20,000-square-foot facility now serves as a center for education and workforce development, while bringing new investment and activity to a key corridor adjacent to Main Street.

items.text: PERRY TOWNSHIP ATHLETIC CODE OF CONDUCT A. Preface The Perry Township Athletic Code of Conduct does not supersede the Student Rights & Responsibilities Policy for Students, Parents, and School Personnel of Perry Township Schools. Individuals may receive discipline under both discipline codes. It is the belief of the coaches, administrators, and school board of Perry Township that participation in athletics is a privilege, not a right, and that as a representative of the school, school system, and community, the athlete is expected to assume certain responsibilities and to live up to certain expectations. It is the purpose of this document to clarify those expectations. A coach may have additional written team rules not addressed in this code. Situations not addressed in this code will be addressed by the building principal. B. The Responsibilities of a Perry Township Athlete: A student/athlete is expected to: 1. Achieve academically to the best of the student’s abilities. Each student’s first responsibility is to be a good student. 2. Act in accordance with high standards of social behavior. 3. Display good sportsmanship both on and off the field. 4. Show respect to opponents, teammates, officials, spectators, coaches, and administrators. 5. Maintain a good appearance including dress, grooming, and cleanliness. 6. Use language that reflects positively on school, community, and family. This includes information shared on social media sites. 7. Be a positive leader in the classroom, on the playing field, in the school, and in the community. 8. Comply with these guidelines in and out of season, on and off the playing field, at school and away from school. C. Eligibility: High School 1. In order to be eligible according to the IHSAA, a student athlete must: a. Have a completed physical form/release form on file with the athletic director of the student’s respective school. b. Have passed five (5) or more full credit subjects during the past grading period and currently enrolled in five (5) or more full credit subjects. 2. If an athlete quits a team while in-season, that athlete is ineligible to participate in another sport unless released by the Athletic Director. This includes pre-season workouts. 31 D. Eligibility: Academy/Middle School (nine-week grade requirements and other eligibility standards) 1. Students in the 6th, 7th, and 8th grade can fail no more than one subject. 2. Students can meet the requirements using either the last nine-week grades of the second semester or the yearly final grades to be eligible for the fall season. 3. A student who is ineligible for the fall season will be permitted to try out for a winter sport provided the student’s grades indicate that the student will be eligible at the end of the first nine-weeks grading period. 4. Perry Meridian Athletics Earns State and National Recognition for Excellence
Perry Meridian High School
By Emily Steinmetz | Jul 31, 2026 9:29 AM
Perry Meridian Athletics Earns State and National Recognition for Excellence Perry Meridian High School Athletics is proud to announce that our athletic department has received two of the highest recognitions available at the state and national levels, affirming our commitment to providing an outstanding education-based athletic experience for every Falcon. For the 2025-2026 school year, Perry Meridian Athletics has been recognized as an IHSAA Sportsmanship Banner School and has also earned the National Interscholastic Athletic Administrators Association (NIAAA) Quality Program Recognition at the Exemplary Level. While championships and victories are celebrated, these honors recognize something even more meaningful—the daily work of building a culture where student-athletes grow as leaders, teammates, and people of character. IHSAA Sportsmanship Banner The Indiana High School Athletic Association (IHSAA) awarded Perry Meridian Athletics its 2025-2026 Sportsmanship Banner, recognizing schools that intentionally promote positive sportsmanship, leadership, and respect throughout their athletic programs. To earn this distinction, schools must demonstrate excellence in four key areas: Outstanding sportsmanship throughout the school year -Student-athlete leadership development -Meaningful community outreach -Intentional efforts to create a positive school culture This recognition reflects the actions of our student-athletes, coaches, parents, administrators, officials, and fans who consistently represent Perry Meridian with integrity and class. National Exemplary Recognition Perry Meridian Athletics has also been selected by the National Interscholastic Athletic Administrators Association (NIAAA) to receive the 2026 Quality Program Recognition at the Exemplary Level—one of the highest honors awarded to high school athletic programs nationwide. The Quality Program Assessment is a comprehensive evaluation of an athletic department's philosophy, leadership, operations, risk management, educational practices, communication, and commitment to continuous improvement. Schools earning the Exemplary distinction provide extensive evidence that their policies, procedures, and daily practices meet the highest professional standards established by the NIAAA. As part of this recognition, Perry Meridian Athletics will be honored during a national ceremony in December, recognized at the 2026 NIAAA National Conference in Phoenix, Arizona, and featured in national publications highlighting exemplary athletic programs across the country. items.title: IHSAA Myths
items.text: IHSAA Myths Let’s debunk the TOP 9 most common Myths and misconceptions about the IHSAA: #1 Myth: The IHSAA is funded by taxpayer dollars. FACT: The IHSAA is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization. We do not receive government funding. Revenue is derived from tournament ticket sales, corporate partnerships, media rights fees, and licensing contest officials. #2 Myth: The IHSAA is a large government organization. FACT: The IHSAA is a small private educational nonprofit with a large impact— overseeing and organizing education-based athletics for 409 voluntary member high schools across all 92 Indiana counties. Our 20 staff members are responsible for administering state tournaments, licensing contest officials, and enforcing our membership’s bylaws in order to maintain fair and equitable learning opportunities in education-based athletics. #3 Myth: The IHSAA Commissioner and Assistant Commissioners create all IHSAA rules. FACT: IHSAA bylaws are created by and voted on by our member schools and their elected representatives(board of directors). All IHSAA staff are hired by those same elected representatives to provide services to our 409 member schools, which includes enforcing our membership’s bylaws and rules. #4 Myth: The IHSAA can change rules at any point and has flexibility in applying rules. FACT: IHSAA rules can only be enacted or changed by a majority vote of the IHSAA board of directors who are elected by the IHSAA member schools they represent. IHSAA staff are bound to apply those rules as written. When our membership wants to change a rule, an appeals process is in place. #5 Myth: The IHSAA realigns Sectionals for team class sports at random. FACT: IHSAA committees audit and scrutinize Sectional alignment every two years, taking many factors into consideration for the entire state rather than any singular area. Committees are made up of superintendents, principals, and athletic directors representing different regions and school sizes around the state. #6 Myth: The IHSAA profits from high school athletics. FACT: Annually, the IHSAA distributes more money back to our membership (over $2.8 million in 2023-24) than we retain for operating costs. For instance, we return 98% of Sectional ticket revenue from our most profitable sports back to our member schools. #7 Myth: The IHSAA always denies athletic eligibility for transfer students. FACT: Annually, 99% of transfer students are granted a path to athletic eligibility. Of our ~160,000 student-athletes, ~4,000 transfer schools (2.5%), and fewer than 50 of those student- athletes are not granted eligibility (1.2% of 2.5%). We always approach transfer cases with the mindset of helping student-athletes find a path to participation, but when eligibility is denied, that decision is made to protect the opportunities of every student-athlete impacted by a transfer. #8 Myth: The IHSAA just runs tournaments that determine the best athletes and teams in the state. FACT: Crowning state champions may be what
